suggestion.rationale: Malware targeting Python users must discover Python installations and site-packages locations. No detection for reconnaissance of Python library paths or version enumeration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on processes querying registry keys related to Python (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Python, HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Python) or invoking 'python -m site', 'pip show', or 'pip list' from unusual parent processes. Flag file system enumerations of site-packages directories.

suggestion.title: SEO Poisoning Click via Search Engine Redirection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'SEO Poisoning to Deliver Fake SQL Developer Malware Installer' as the initial compromise vector. Pipeline produced no detection for this entry point.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect clicks from search engine results (referrer: google.com, bing.com, etc.) followed by suspicious downloads of .msi or .exe files containing 'SQL' in the filename, particularly from newly registered or low-reputation domains. Correlate with browser child processes spawning installers.

suggestion.title: Suspicious SQL Developer Installer Execution from Downloads Folder
suggestion.rationale: Article describes delivery as 'Fake SQL Developer Malware Installer'; execution of masqueraded installers is a core attack step. No execution-phase detection suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor execution of .msi or .exe files claiming to be SQL Server Developer Edition or similar Microsoft tools from user Downloads folder with low code-signing scores or unsigned. Alert on parent process = explorer.exe or browser, particularly if installer size/entropy anomalous for official Microsoft binaries.

suggestion.title: SQL Installer Spawning Suspicious Child Processes
suggestion.rationale: Malware-as-installer campaigns typically use the installer shim to execute hidden payloads. No post-execution child-process monitoring suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect child processes spawned by SQL Developer or similar database tool installers that are: unsigned, non-Microsoft binaries, powershell.exe with script-block execution, or processes spawning network connections to non-Microsoft C2 infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Malware Persistence via Database Tool Registry Modifications
suggestion.rationale: Fake installer delivery implies persistence or follow-on payload execution; article does not provide specifics, but registry-based persistence common in APT campaigns. No persistence-phase detection generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor registry write operations under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, Run Once, and Startup folders for suspicious entries with file paths pointing to malware binaries or scripts executed during SQL Developer installer execution. Flag entries with obfuscated command lines or non-existent file references.

suggestion.title: Kazuar Modular Component Loader Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Modular Espionage Ecosystem'—suggests multi-component architecture with plugin/loader pattern. No detection use case was generated despite this being core to the threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect process launches with unusual library injection patterns or spawning of child processes from temporary directories. Kazuar's modular design likely involves reflective DLL injection or process hollowing to load espionage plugins. Monitor for parent-child process chains from system utilities executing from unusual paths.

suggestion.title: Kazuar Command & Control Channel Beaconing
suggestion.rationale: Title references 'Espionage Ecosystem' operations—implies sustained C2 communication for data exfiltration. No detection for network-based C2 communication was generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on suspicious outbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic from compromised endpoints to low-reputation IP addresses or domains with long DNS TTLs. Espionage malware typically establishes persistent C2 channels. Look for beaconing patterns: regular interval connections, small request/large response asymmetry, or connections to newly registered domains.

suggestion.title: Kazuar Credential/Data Harvesting Process Chain
suggestion.rationale: Espionage-focused malware 'ecosystem' implies credential theft and data collection phases. No use cases for discovery/collection techniques were provided.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for processes accessing known credential stores (lsass.exe, SAM hive, Chromium profile databases), performing clipboard monitoring APIs, or screenshotting/recording capabilities. Kazuar's espionage focus suggests it harvests both credentials and sensitive screen content. Trigger on unexpected processes calling BitBlt, GetClipboardData, or accessing %APPDATA%\Google\Chrome\.

suggestion.title: Kazuar Ecosystem Stage-2 Payload Delivery
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'evolves into' and 'ecosystem'—implies staged delivery, initial dropper plus modular components. No detection for multi-stage infection flow was specified.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect initial access vector (likely spear-phishing attachment or exploit) followed by suspicious child process spawning or file downloads from attacker-controlled infrastructure. Look for email-spawned processes (outlook.exe → cmd.exe → powershell.exe → download), temporary file creation in %APPDATA% or %TEMP%, and subsequent network requests from unfamiliar binaries.

suggestion.title: Persistence Mechanism for Kazuar Re-infection
suggestion.rationale: 'Secret Blizzard Operations' implies long-term dwell time. No detection use cases for persistence (scheduled tasks, registry modifications, WMI event subscriptions) were generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for suspicious scheduled task creation (especially with .NET assemblies or obfuscated payloads), unusual registry modification in Run/RunOnce keys or AppInit_DLLs, or WMI event subscription creation targeting process execution. Espionage malware requires persistence across reboots; look for system-level modifications executed by medium-integrity processes.

suggestion.title: Defense Evasion: Kazuar UAC Bypass & AMSI Evasion
suggestion.rationale: Modular espionage ecosystem implies sophisticated evasion techniques to maintain persistence against security controls. No detection for UAC bypass or antimalware evasion was proposed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on processes modifying HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System to disable UAC, attempting to access WinRM/COM elevation mechanisms, or invoking PowerShell with -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden and suspicious encoded scripts. Monitor for patching of amsi.dll or loading of untrusted security providers.

suggestion.title: KnowledgeDeliver LMS zero-day exploitation attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article headline: 'KnowledgeDeliver LMS Zero-Day Exploited'. Pipeline extracted no initial-access detection despite explicit vulnerability mention.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP requests to KnowledgeDeliver LMS instances with malformed parameters, unusual payload sizes, or known zero-day exploitation signatures. Alert on successful file uploads to web-accessible paths immediately after suspicious POST requests.

suggestion.title: BLUEBEAM web shell detection and execution

Monitor for suspicious child process execution spawned by web server processes (w3wp.exe, httpd, apache2) with high-entropy or encoded command-line arguments.

suggestion.title: Web shell command execution via HTTP
suggestion.rationale: Web shell deployment inherently leads to command execution via HTTP requests. Pipeline generated no C2 or execution detection rules.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP POST requests to suspicious paths with encoded payloads, unusual User-Agent strings, or POST parameters containing command-like strings (cmd.exe, powershell, bash). Correlate with anomalous child process spawning from web server processes.

suggestion.title: Suspicious file upload to KnowledgeDeliver directories
suggestion.rationale: Web shell deployment requires file upload/write. Article describes exploit leading to shell deployment but pipeline suggested no file-activity detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unexpected file creation in KnowledgeDeliver LMS directories (especially web-accessible paths) with .php, .aspx, .jsp, or .sh extensions. Correlate with prior HTTP POST requests lacking legitimate upload context.

suggestion.title: Lazarus RemotePE Process Injection Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'memory-only RAT'—implying code injection or process hollowing, never disk writes. Pipeline missed detection for unsigned code execution in process memory.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for suspicious process creation with empty command line, parent-child process anomalies (e.g., legitimate process spawning encoded PowerShell), or VirtualAlloc + WriteProcessMemory combinations. Alert on processes loading unsigned DLLs from unexpected paths.

suggestion.title: Lazarus RAT Command & Control Beaconing

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting Post-RemotePE Execution
suggestion.rationale: RATs targeting financial firms typically pivot to credential theft (LSASS dump, SAM, registry). Article states crypto/finance targets but pipeline extracted zero credential-access techniques.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect uncommon command-line invocations of mimikatz, lsass.exe dumping, or hive registry reads. Alert on suspicious access patterns to HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SAM and SECURITY hives immediately after unsigned code injection events. Look for process execution from temp/downloads.

suggestion.title: Lazarus Malware Family Hashing & Detonation

suggestion.title: Financial/Crypto Sector Targeting Behavioral Correlation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly targets financial and cryptocurrency firms. Pipeline failed to generate industry-vertical detection rules linking Lazarus targeting patterns to these sectors.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag spear-phishing emails with financial/crypto-industry lures, suspicious attachments, or lookalike domains targeting known finance/exchange employees. Cross-reference against Lazarus OSINT indicators: typosquatting of exchange/broker domains, malicious Office macros with PE headers.

suggestion.title: Lazarus Persistence via Scheduled Tasks and Registry Runs

suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for new scheduled task creation with suspicious triggers (esp. SYSTEM/NETWORK SERVICE context), binary execution from temp/user-writable paths, or registry modifications to HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services and HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with unsigned payloads.

suggestion.title: Gemini Prompt Injection / Jailbreak Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'jailbroken Gemini' as initial attack vector. Pipeline failed to generate detection for prompt injection patterns, DAN mode activation, system-prompt override attempts, or jailbreak keywords in API requests.

suggestion.title: LLM-Assisted Credential Harvesting

suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Gemini queries requesting credential formats, admin account lists, password patterns, or auth bypass techniques. suggestion.title: Cryptocurrency Wallet Transaction Spike / Unauthorized Drain
suggestion.rationale: Article title specifies 'drain crypto wallets' as primary impact. Pipeline produced no financial/blockchain use case for detecting rapid unauthorized wallet transactions, transfers to external addresses, or mixing service deposits.

suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag Gemini API tokens used from geographically impossible locations, IPs inconsistent with known admin infrastructure, or token reuse across multiple user identities. Alert on token activity spike post-compromise or tokens used outside normal business patterns.

suggestion.title: Admin Privileged Account Lateral Access
suggestion.rationale: Stolen admin credentials enable lateral movement and privilege escalation. Pipeline should detect unauthorized admin logins, privilege elevation, or lateral access but generated no use cases for post-compromise admin abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor compromised admin account for logons from untrusted IPs, VPNs, or geolocations inconsistent with baseline. Alert on rapid authentication failures followed by success, MFA bypass attempts, or privilege elevation immediately post-compromise.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Code Generation via Jailbroken LLM

suggestion.title: Suspicious Package Installation from Malicious Repository

suggestion.title: Credential Access via Post-Installation Script Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'credential-stealing malware' — this implies install-time execution of hooks or post-install scripts. Supply chain attacks commonly abuse npm postinstall, PyPI setup.py, or Cargo build scripts.

suggestion.title: Exfiltration of SSH Keys or Git Credentials Post-Package Install
suggestion.rationale: Credential-stealing malware typically targets developer environments where SSH keys and .git credentials live. Article does not detail exfiltration mechanism but title implies data theft.

suggestion.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via 7-Zip Archive Processing

suggestion.title: Malicious Archive Delivery and Open

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation File Activity from 7-Zip Context

suggestion.title: termsrv.dll File Modification or Replacement Detection

Flag bulk registrations or those immediately following inbox rule creation activity.

suggestion.rationale: Abuse of token type: device code flow tokens are designed for limited-capability devices (printers, IoT, TVs); detecting their use for rich interactive cloud services reveals compromise. Correlate file-open events with child spawn to confirm decompression trigger. Baseline legitimate archive workflows; flag execution from temp directories or with obfuscated arguments.

suggestion.title: Malicious Archive File Delivery and Execution Chain
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attacker-controlled archives as attack vector ('Let Attackers Execute'); pipeline did not surface initial-access detection for archive receipt/user interaction.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag archives (7z, zip) created in user Downloads, Temp, or Documents directories immediately followed by extraction and child-process spawning. Alert on archives with suspicious naming (mimicking documents) or received from external email sources. Correlate file-timestamps to user logon time for delivered-malware patterns.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable 7-Zip Version Exploitation Indicator
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'New 7-Zip Vulnerabilities'—pipeline must extract affected versions and CVE IDs for baseline comparison. Zero version indicators extracted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Inventory 7-Zip installations via file version metadata (7z.exe ProductVersion). Cross-reference against published CVE version ranges. Alert on execution of vulnerable versions combined with suspicious archive handling. Prioritize endpoints with vulnerable 7-Zip + default UAC settings + no EDR.

suggestion.title: Memory Corruption Signature in 7-Zip Process
suggestion.rationale: Code-execution vulnerabilities typically trigger memory safety issues before payload execution. Pipeline ignored behavioral indicators of memory exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for 7z.exe performing unusual memory operations: VirtualAllocEx with EXECUTE permissions, WriteProcessMemory calls, or DLL injection patterns. Flag 7z.exe loading unexpected DLLs (non-msvcrt, non-kernel). Detect heap spraying indicators (rapid memory allocation followed by code execution).

suggestion.title: System Compromise Post-Archive: Registry and Privilege Escalation
suggestion.rationale: Article headline claims 'Compromise Systems'—pipeline failed to detect post-exploitation persistence and privilege escalation typical of arbitrary-code-execution exploits.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate 7-Zip execution with subsequent HKLM registry modification attempts, UAC bypass techniques, or SYSTEM-context child processes. Flag RunOnce/Run registry writes, Scheduled Task creation, or service installation within 30 seconds of archive extraction. Alert on token impersonation or SeImpersonatePrivilege escalation.

suggestion.title: Encoded Payload Staging in Archive Containers
suggestion.rationale: Attack flow requires attackers to embed executable payloads in archives; pipeline did not detect archive content anomalies or staging patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect archives containing obfuscated/encoded scripts (base64, hex-encoded PowerShell), double-extensions (.txt.exe), or binaries in nested directories (.\..\..\payload.exe). Flag archives with anomalous compression ratios or archived archives (zip-in-7z patterns). Monitor 7-Zip temp extraction paths for suspicious file writes.

suggestion.title: termsrv.dll File Modification Detection
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states 'Modifies termsrv.dll' — zero detection rules generated. File-integrity monitoring on System32/termsrv.dll is the core detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on write or modify operations to termsrv.dll or termsrv.dll.bak in System32. Validate file hash against known-good baselines from Windows Update catalogs. Correlate modifications with RDP service restart or unexpected service activation.

suggestion.title: RDP Terminal Services Registry Modification for Session Bypass
suggestion.rationale: Enabling multiple concurrent RDP sessions requires registry changes (e.g., fSingleSessionPerUser=0, MaxInstanceCount); article's technique implies registry persistence—no detection generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect modifications to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server registry tree, especially fSingleSessionPerUser, MaxInstanceCount, or licensing subkeys. Flag when paired with termsrv.dll access events.

suggestion.title: Multiple Concurrent RDP Sessions Anomaly Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title: technique enables 'Multiple RDP Sessions'—no post-compromise detection for abuse of this capability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor 4624 (Logon Type 10/RDP) and 4778 (RDP Session Reconnect) events. Flag when single source IP initiates >1 concurrent RDP sessions within 5 minute window, or when session count anomalously exceeds baseline per workstation.

suggestion.title: RDP Service Code Injection or Unsigned DLL Load
suggestion.rationale: Persistence via DLL patching may involve service injection; article describes modification but no monitor for T1547 (autostart execution via service hijacking) or unsigned process loads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor svchost.exe -k termsvcs for unsigned or anomalous DLL loads. Alert on CreateRemoteThread targeting RDP service process. Detect image-load events on non-standard or unsigned DLL variants in System32.

suggestion.title: Cloud Atlas Campaign File Hash Baseline and Delivery Chain
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline IOCs output is empty object {}; article title names actor but no hash values, file names, or delivery indicators extracted from campaign.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish golden image hashes for termsrv.dll across Windows Server 2016/2019/2022 and Windows 10/11 builds. Generate alerts on hash mismatches. Cross-reference with Cloud Atlas C2 infrastructure (if available from prior intel) and known delivery TTPs.

suggestion.title: Bank account creation anomalies matching mule account profiles
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'verified bank and fintech mule accounts' being sold, implying accounts are being created with false identities or rapidly activated with minimal legitimate use. Title establishes the end-product: accounts pre-configured for fraud use.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor banking/fintech platforms for account creation patterns with zero to minimal legitimate transaction history within 24-48 hours of activation. Flag accounts created via third-party credential, unusual geographic velocity, or multiple accounts from same device/IP. Correlate account holder identity verification artifacts with known fraud indicators.

suggestion.title: Telegram channel activity indicative of credential trading marketplaces
suggestion.rationale: Article title directly states 'Telegram Channels to Sell Verified Bank and Fintech Mule Accounts'. This is an explicit C2/marketplace infrastructure play. Defenders should detect access to known credential trading channels or indicators of account credential exfiltration destined for Telegram.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag network traffic to Telegram API endpoints or Telegram desktop/web client coupled with unusual data exfiltration patterns (credential dumps, account lists). Monitor for suspicious Telegram group/channel joins preceded by credential harvesting activity or account enumeration on banking platforms.

suggestion.title: Mule account behavioral anomalies post-compromise
suggestion.rationale: Mule accounts are compromised or created accounts used specifically for money laundering/fraud. The article's premise—that accounts are being 'sold'—implies they will be used for high-risk transactions. Defenders should detect behavioral divergence from legitimate account use.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After account creation or initial compromise, monitor for rapid high-value transactions, cross-border wire transfers, frequent login/logout cycles from new geographies, or access patterns inconsistent with account profile. Flag accounts that receive funds then immediately forward them (circular transaction patterns).

suggestion.title: Credential harvesting targeting bank customer identity information
suggestion.rationale: To 'sell verified' accounts, criminals must first harvest or create identities and link them to functioning bank accounts. Article's emphasis on 'verified' suggests phishing or social engineering for KYC/identity data. Pipeline missed T1598/T1589 mapping entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for phishing campaigns targeting customers of major fintech/banking platforms (credential theft, KYC document exfiltration). Detect reconnaissance activity (account enumeration, identity lookups) preceding account creation bursts. Flag bulk requests for identity verification or account activation flows.

suggestion.title: Device Code Authentication Flow Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states Kali365 'abuses OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization grant flow' and 'threat actors initiate the device authorization process themselves to generate a code, then trick targets into entering it on Microsoft's login page.' This is the primary attack vector requiring detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect anomalous device code authentication patterns: service principals or user accounts initiating device code flows that don't normally authenticate this way. Flag multiple failed device code attempts followed by success, multiple users entering the same device code, or device code authentication from unusual geographic locations followed by successful mailbox access.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Inbox Rules Creation Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'attackers...created malicious inbox rules designed to hide their activity.' This is direct evidence of persistence and defense evasion activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect creation or modification of inbox rules that redirect, delete, move, or forward emails—especially rules marked as hidden or applying to all messages. Alert on rules created by newly-compromised accounts immediately after successful device code authentication, particularly those forwarding to external domains.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Device Registration in Microsoft Entra
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'attackers also registered new devices in victims' Microsoft environments, further extending their access to the breached network.' Device registration is a direct persistence mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect anomalous device registrations: multiple devices registered by a single user account within 24 hours, device registration from unexpected locations, or registration events immediately following device code authentication success. Flag suspicious device names or registrations from non-corporate MAC vendors.

suggestion.title: Session Token Capture via Adversary-in-the-Middle Proxy
suggestion.rationale: Article describes Kali365's 'Cookie Link' mode that 'proxies victims through attacker-controlled infrastructure that captures authenticated browser sessions, session cookies, and tokens.' This represents active session hijacking.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect signs of AitM proxy attacks: authentication succeeding through unexpected proxy infrastructure or CDNs, successful authentication followed by access from different IP within minutes, unusual User-Agent patterns during login, or access tokens used from divergent geolocation within same session.

suggestion.title: Phishing Campaign Targeting Device Code Portal
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'phishing emails that directed victims to Microsoft's device code login portal (http://microsoft.com/devicelogin), where they unknowingly authorized attackers to access their accounts.' Detecting these phishing emails is critical initial access defense.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect phishing emails containing links to or references to Microsoft device code login portal with urgency language ('verify account', 'confirm identity', 'unusual sign-in'). Flag high-volume external phishing campaigns from suspicious senders impersonating Microsoft, and emails requesting users to enter device codes.

suggestion.title: Rapid Device Enrollment Cascade Post-Token Theft
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attackers gaining 'full access to their account without requiring MFA challenges' then immediately registering multiple devices. This chained activity (token theft → device registration) is a high-confidence compromise indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect correlated anomalies: successful device code authentication immediately followed by device registration within 15 minutes, or a single compromised account registering 3+ devices within 24 hours from different IPs. Flag device registration events at off-hours or from geographic locations inconsistent with user history.

suggestion.title: Detect CVE-2026-26980 Ghost CMS Exploitation Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly cites vulnerability and product; pipeline extracted zero IOCs despite 'CVE-2026-26980 Exploited' being primary attack vector
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP requests to Ghost CMS admin routes (e.g., /ghost/api/v3/, /admin/) containing payloads targeting known CVE-2026-26980 bypass patterns, file upload requests to theme directories, or SQL injection signatures. suggestion.title: Detect ClickFix Scareware Injection in Web Responses

suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect injection of ClickFix-characteristic JavaScript or HTML patterns in web responses from Ghost CMS instances: inline scripts with crypto-mining, fake browser alert boxes, tech-support phone numbers, or external script loads from known ClickFix C2 domains. suggestion.title: Detect Mass Ghost CMS Compromise via Pattern Correlation
suggestion.rationale: Title specifies 700+ sites compromised indicating coordinated campaign; pipeline should flag breadth-of-compromise pattern rather than single-site detections
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate exploitation signatures across 50+ distinct domains within 24-hour window: same CVE exploitation path, identical ClickFix payload variants, shared C2 infrastructure, or synchronized content modifications. Flag as mass-compromise campaign.

suggestion.title: Detect Ghost CMS Version Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Attackers typically enumerate CMS versions before exploiting CVE; article implies targeted attacks on Ghost but pipeline generated no reconnaissance-phase detection
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect requests to Ghost-specific endpoints that leak version info (e.g., /ghost/api/v3/admin/site/, /assets/built/version.txt, theme.json parsing, or sitemap.xml fingerprinting) when followed by exploit attempts within 1 hour.

suggestion.title: Detect Malicious Payloads Delivered via Legitimate CDN Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article core claim: attackers 'abuse shared CDN infrastructure to bypass domain reputation security controls'—requires detection of malicious content served from known-good CDN IP ranges (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, etc.) bound to reputation-filtered domains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for file downloads/executions from CDN provider IPs where the target domain has known-poor reputation or is on internal block lists. Correlate high-reputation CDN IP with low-reputation destination domain. Flag binary/script payloads delivered this way.

suggestion.title: Domain Reputation Filtering Bypass via CDN Shared IP
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states bypass of 'domain reputation security controls'—detection should identify previously-blocked domains now accessible because they resolve to shared CDN infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track DNS resolutions of domains in reputation blocklists that point to major CDN CIDR blocks. Alert on connection attempts to these domains after CDN redirection. Baseline legitimate CDN-hosted content at same IPs to reduce false positives.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Request Patterns from High-Reputation CDN IPs
suggestion.rationale: Attackers leverage 'shared CDN infrastructure'—legitimate CDN traffic has predictable patterns; anomalies (malformed headers, binary payloads, suspicious User-Agents) indicate abuse for evasion.

suggestion.title: CDN IP Infrastructure Used for Command-and-Control
suggestion.rationale: Attackers abuse CDN to hide C2 traffic behind legitimate reputation—detection should identify beaconing patterns or suspicious callback behavior from CDN-hosted endpoints.

Correlate with known malware families using CDN-based C2. Compare traffic patterns against legitimate CDN usage baseline.

suggestion.title: SSH-Like Filename Masquerading During Package Installation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes payload hidden under 'SSH-Like Filename During Package Installation.' This is direct T1036.005 masquerading: malicious files assume names of legitimate SSH utilities to evade inspection during package manager operations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor file creation events during package installation (apt, yum, rpm, pip) for filenames matching SSH-related patterns (ssh, sshd, ssh_config, authorized_keys, id_rsa) created in non-standard directories or with suspicious owners/permissions. Correlate file writes with unexpected parent processes (curl, wget, python, perl).

suggestion.title: Payload Execution via Package Manager Hook/Dependency Resolution
suggestion.rationale: Article states payload is hidden 'during package installation'—indicating exploitation of installation workflows (pre/post-install scripts, dependency resolution hooks) to trigger arbitrary code execution. Classic supply-chain execution vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unexpected child processes spawned by package managers during install/update operations that establish network connections, write to /root or /var/spool, or execute shell commands with obfuscated arguments. Flag short-lived processes with randomized names spawned by apt/yum/pip post-install handlers.

suggestion.title: Non-Standard Package Repository Configuration
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attacks via package installation typically involve either compromised official packages or installation from untrusted sources. Detection must cover repository swaps, custom indexes, or unusual package sources.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor modifications to /etc/apt/sources.list*, /etc/yum.repos.d/, pip.conf, and ~/.npmrc for additions of non-standard repositories. Alert on package installation commands using --index-url, --extra-index-url, or explicit source parameters pointing outside organizational allowlists.

suggestion.title: File Attribute Anomalies in Package-Installed Objects
suggestion.rationale: Obfuscated payloads masquerading as system utilities will exhibit suspicious metadata inconsistencies (wrong UID, missing expected execute permissions, unexpected timestamps, unusual file sizes compared to legitimate utility baselines).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Profile legitimate package installations to establish baseline file attributes (owner, permissions, size, hash) for known utilities. Flag deviations: mismatched ownership, execute bit missing/present unexpectedly, file size divergence from known-good, or modification timestamps inconsistent with package metadata.

suggestion.title: Execution of .pyd and .so Files from Suspicious Paths
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly establishes malware 'ships as .pyd and .so files to evade script detection'—compiled extensions are the core evasion mechanism. This is the primary attack vector and should have generated a use case immediately.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on .pyd (Python extension, Windows) and .so (shared object, Linux) execution from user directories, %TEMP%, AppData, or downloads. Correlate with Python interpreter invocation or direct binary execution. Baseline legitimate extensions (numpy, scipy) by publisher signature and execution context.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Creation of Compiled Extensions in Runtime Directories
suggestion.rationale: Malware that evades script detection by using compiled code typically stages the extension in runtime temp paths before execution. Article's emphasis on evasion implies multi-stage delivery.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect rapid file creation of .pyd or .so followed by execution within 10 seconds in %TEMP%, /tmp, AppData Local Temp, or user profile subdirectories. Flag unsigned or stripped-symbol binaries.

suggestion.title: Unsigned or Stripped-Metadata Python Extension Execution
suggestion.rationale: Phrase 'evade script detection' implies obfuscation and anti-forensic packaging. Legitimate Python extensions carry vendor signatures; InvisibleFerret variants should lack standard code-signing or contain suspicious metadata.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor .pyd/.so execution with missing or invalid code signatures, no publisher info, or obfuscated PE/ELF headers. Correlate with .pyd/.so load events lacking standard Python package directories.

suggestion.title: Python Process Loading Unexpected Compiled Extensions
suggestion.rationale: Evasion pattern: legitimate Python script triggers malicious compiled extension. Core tactic implied by 'ships as .pyd and .so'—suggests split payloads designed to bypass script-based detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Python interpreter loading .pyd/.so modules from non-standard site-packages, user writable paths, or network locations. Baseline by process (python.exe, python3), and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: InvisibleFerret IOC Hunting and Correlation
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline failed to extract even the malware name 'InvisibleFerret' as an identifier. This should be a searchable IOC across file paths, registry, command-line artifacts, and threat feeds.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt file systems, event logs, and threat-intel feeds for 'InvisibleFerret' strings, variant names, and associated hashes or C2 domains. Cross-correlate with .pyd/.so execution events to identify infected systems.

suggestion.title: SEO Poisoning — Spoofed Developer-Tool Domains
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly: 'SEO poisoning to deliver fake SQL developer malware installer.' Must detect newly-registered domains mimicking SQL tools (SQL Server Management Studio, SQLDeveloper, Oracle SQL Developer) appearing in organic search results.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify DNS queries and HTTP GETs to domains containing SQL-related keywords (sqldev, sqldeveloper, sqlserver) registered <30 days. Cross-reference against known legitimate SQL vendor domains (microsoft.com, oracle.com) to flag homographs and typosquats in search results.

suggestion.title: Trojanized Installer Execution from User-Writable Directories
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'fake SQL developer malware installer.' Must detect .exe or .msi files with SQL-naming conventions executing from Downloads, Temp, AppData—standard staging ground for trojanized software.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process creation where image path includes '*\Downloads\*sql*.exe' or '%temp%\*sqldev*.msi' and parent is explorer.exe or cmd.exe. Inspect command-line for encoding/obfuscation and unusual working directories.

suggestion.title: Malicious Child Process Spawning from Installer
suggestion.rationale: Trojanized installer drops payload and executes it. Must detect unsigned/suspicious child processes (rundll32.exe, powershell.exe, cmd.exe /c) spawned within minutes of installer execution, or registry persistence writes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate SQL installer execution with spawning of rundll32.exe, powershell.exe, or cmd.exe within 5-minute window. Flag registry modifications under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Run or System startup directories from installer process or descendants.

suggestion.title: Command-and-Control Beaconing Post-Infection
suggestion.rationale: Malware payload will establish C2 communication. Must detect outbound connections from installer/child processes to non-standard ports (>10000) or newly-registered/suspicious domains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound network connections from SQL installer and spawned children to non-HTTP/HTTPS ports or domains with WHOIS age <30 days or high-entropy names. Baseline against known Microsoft/Oracle infrastructure.

suggestion.title: File Hash Detection — Trojanized SQL Installers
suggestion.rationale: Article describes malware distribution but pipeline extracted zero file hashes. Must capture MD5/SHA-256 of observed trojanized installers from article, vendor advisories (Mandiant, CISA), or internal quarantine logs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Ingest file hashes from threat feed, vendor advisories, or EDR quarantine. Alert on any file creation or download matching malicious hash list via endpoint telemetry or firewall logs.

suggestion.title: KnowledgeDeliver LMS RCE Exploitation

Alert on non-standard request patterns to LMS administrative or upload handlers, especially if followed by unusual process spawning or web shell file creation.

suggestion.title: BLUEBEAM Web Shell Deployment and Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly mentions 'BLUEBEAM Web Shell' as the post-exploitation payload. No IOCs or use cases generated for malware detection or web shell behavior. Pipeline missed the core attack outcome.

Monitor for HTTP requests with suspicious parameter names or obfuscated payloads referencing 'BLUEBEAM' or file paths consistent with web shell staging locations.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Web Shell Command Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article describes BLUEBEAM web shell deployment but pipeline generated no persistence or command-execution detection. Web shells require follow-on activity (reconnaissance, data collection, lateral movement) that should trigger detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP POST/GET requests containing shell command syntax (whoami, ipconfig, dir, curl, wget, net commands) sent to known or suspected web shell paths. Correlate with outbound network connections from w3wp.exe or IIS worker processes to external IPs/domains.

suggestion.title: LMS Data Exfiltration via Web Shell
suggestion.rationale: KnowledgeDeliver is an LMS (learning management system) containing sensitive student/course data. Article does not detail post-shell actions but pipeline should anticipate collection and exfiltration use cases typical of LMS compromises.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for SQL queries or file reads from LMS database tables (users, course enrollments, grades) initiated by IIS processes. Detect large HTTP responses from web server to external IPs, or compression/archival activity targeting LMS data directories.

suggestion.title: RemotePE Memory-Only RAT Process Injection Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'memory-only RAT' — requires detection of in-memory code execution and process injection without on-disk artifacts. Pipeline should flag: shellcode execution from unsigned memory regions, remote thread creation into legitimate processes, and syscall-based injection patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual memory allocation patterns (VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory) to legitimate system processes (svchost, explorer, lsass). Flag process creation with mismatched parent or command line, combined with remote memory writes in adjacent processes. Memory-only payloads often inject into running processes leaving minimal filesystem artifacts.

suggestion.title: Lazarus Lazarus Spearphishing with RemotePE Delivery
suggestion.rationale: Lazarus historically uses spearphishing for initial access. Article targets 'financial and crypto firms' (likely email-delivered compromise). Should detect suspicious attachment delivery, macro/script execution chains.

Flag unusual child processes spawned from Office applications or scripting hosts; RemotePE delivery often chains: email → macro → PowerShell/cmd → shellcode injection.

suggestion.title: C2 Callback Detection for RemotePE RAT
suggestion.rationale: Memory-only RAT must establish C2 post-injection. Article describes attacks on crypto/finance — expect encrypted HTTPS or obfuscated HTTP callbacks. Pipeline should suggest network detection for unknown outbound HTTPS to private/bulletproof hosting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate process injection (svchost/explorer) with new HTTPS outbound connections to unknown ASNs. Flag long-lived encrypted sessions from unlikely processes. RemotePE payloads typically use encrypted C2 channels; baseline legitimate HTTPS destinations and alert on new ones.

suggestion.title: Lazarus Tooling: HaE, MATA, DTrack Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Historical Lazarus playbooks include living-off-the-land discovery (ipconfig, tasklist, whoami) and lateral movement tools. Article describes 'financial firms' — suggests credential harvesting and internal reconnaissance.

suggestion.title: Credential Dumping via LSASS Process Access
suggestion.rationale: Crypto/financial theft operations require credential harvesting. Article targeting 'financial firms' suggests LSASS/SAM dumping for account takeover.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unsigned/suspicious processes (rundll32, regsvcs, msiexec) opening LSASS with suspicious access masks (0x1fffff = full access). suggestion.title: Defense Evasion: UAC Bypass and Payload Obfuscation

suggestion.title: Anomalous Administrative Credential Access via Compromised AI Interface

suggestion.title: Cryptocurrency Wallet Access Following Credential Compromise

suggestion.title: Bulk Credential Exfiltration via AI API Logs
suggestion.rationale: The attack chain required extracting 'admin credentials' from protected systems. Pipeline lacks detection for mass credential enumeration, file read operations targeting credential stores, or encoded exfil within API responses.

suggestion.title: Administrative Account Privilege Escalation Post-AI Compromise

Monitor Active Directory or IAM logs for role assignments or capability additions granted via programmatic APIs correlated with AI jailbreak timestamps.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Process Spawning from AI Service Context
suggestion.rationale: Execution via jailbroken model likely required spawning child processes (credential dumping, wallet CLI tools). Pipeline missed process-creation detections linked to AI API activity.

Flag execution of credential-dumping utilities (mimikatz, pypykatz), wallet tools (geth, ethers.js), or file-read utilities issued by service accounts tied to LLM inference.

suggestion.title: Malicious Package Installation from Public Registries
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attack via npm, PyPI, and CratesIO indicates attacker-controlled packages hosted on public repositories; article title explicitly names the attack vector.

suggestion.title: Post-Install Hook Execution - Credential Theft
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain malware typically executes via post-install scripts; article specifies credential-stealing behavior as payload.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on node_modules/.bin/*, setup.py script execution, or build.rs execution immediately following package installation. Monitor for spawning of shell interpreters (bash, powershell, cmd.exe) from package directories.

suggestion.title: Credential Access via Malicious Package Dependencies
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states credential-stealing malware; this represents the credential access phase of the attack chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for processes spawned by package managers accessing credential stores (.aws/credentials, .git/credentials, .ssh), environment variables, or password managers. Alert on exfiltration of bulk credential data.

suggestion.title: Package Registry Tampering Detection
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attacks compromise package metadata and availability; detection should cover registry-side anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Verify package hashes, signatures, and metadata against upstream registries. Alert on unexpected version updates, author changes, or packages re-uploaded with modified content.

suggestion.title: Multi-Ecosystem Supply Chain Attack - npm, PyPI, Crates
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names three separate package ecosystems; this indicates coordinated, multi-language attack infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate suspicious package installations across npm, PyPI, and Crates.io; look for patterns suggesting same attacker (shared metadata, timing, download patterns, malware signatures across implementations).

suggestion.title: 7-Zip Archive Extraction Followed by Child Process Spawning
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes 'Execute Arbitrary Code' attack—execution occurs during archive extraction/parsing. Pipeline missed obvious process-tree detection for 7z.exe or 7zG.exe spawning suspicious child processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor 7z.exe or 7zG.exe spawning unexpected child processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, regsvcs.exe, or network-facing utilities) with shortened parent-to-child time delta. Legitimate archive operations rarely spawn children; RCE exploitation will require command interpreter.

suggestion.title: Suspicious 7-Zip File Association Triggering Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article title implies user opens/extracts malicious archive triggering code execution. Pipeline missed detection for file-association exploitation or handler registration abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag anomalous 7z file delivery via email or USB (DeviceFileEvents from non-standard locations), especially with double-extensions or obfuscated names. Correlate with immediate 7z.exe invocation and unexpected child-process lineage.

suggestion.title: 7-Zip Process Memory Injection or Unsigned DLL Load
suggestion.rationale: Code execution in 7-Zip context may occur via memory corruption or DLL injection rather than spawning children. Article does not explicitly exclude in-process RCE.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor 7z.exe loading unsigned or unsigned-from-unusual-paths DLLs, or DLLs from temp/user-writable locations. Look for API call sequences (LoadLibrary, GetProcAddress) in memory telemetry if available.

suggestion.title: Exploitation-Pattern Network Activity from 7-Zip Process
suggestion.rationale: If RCE achieved, attacker may pivot immediately; pipeline missed network-egress detection. No article text provided but standard for code-execution vulns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag 7z.exe or spawned children initiating outbound connections to suspicious domains/IPs (not legitimate 7-Zip update servers). Unusual ports (4444, 5555, 8888), or connections to geolocations inconsistent with environment.

suggestion.title: Exploitation via Malicious Archive Filename or Zip-Slip Path Traversal
suggestion.rationale: 7-Zip vulnerabilities historically include path-traversal bugs (CVE-2024-24919 class). Pipeline did not surface detection for extraction of files to privileged paths or system directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for 7-Zip extraction writing files to C:\Windows, C:\Program Files, TEMP paths with .exe/.sys/.bat/.vbs, or creating symlinks/junctions. Compare archive member paths against extraction destinations for traversal patterns.

suggestion.title: Detect termsrv.dll File Modification or Replacement
suggestion.rationale: Article core claim: 'Modifies termsrv.dll to Enable Multiple RDP Sessions.' This is the attack vector and must be detectable via file integrity monitoring.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any write, modification, or replacement of C:\Windows\System32\termsrv.dll. Establish baseline hash of legitimate termsrv.dll per OS version and alert on hash mismatches. Correlate with failed RDP logon attempts or unusual RDP port activity to increase signal.

suggestion.title: Detect Multiple Concurrent RDP Sessions per User
suggestion.rationale: Article states the attack 'Enable Multiple RDP Sessions on Victim Hosts'—multiple simultaneous RDP sessions per user is anomalous and signals that termsrv.dll modification succeeded.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for two or more concurrent RDP sessions (EventID 4778 or RDP session logs) established under the same user account within a short window. Baseline normal session counts; flag service accounts or domain admin accounts with multiple sessions outside business hours.

suggestion.title: Detect RDP fSingleSessionPerUser Registry Modification
suggestion.rationale: Enabling multi-session RDP requires setting registry value fSingleSessionPerUser to 0 in HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server; this is a prerequisite to the termsrv.dll attack.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on administrative modification of HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\fSingleSessionPerUser, particularly when set to 0 (or deletion of the value). Correlate with termsrv.dll modification for high-confidence persistence chain.

suggestion.title: Detect termsrv.dll Modification + RDP Logon Correlation
suggestion.rationale: The attack combines two signals: DLL tampering + RDP multi-session enablement. Correlation rule closes detection gaps in both.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Build a rule that triggers when termsrv.dll file modification (from monitoring) occurs within 10 minutes of a successful RDP logon (EventID 4624, Logon Type 10) on the same host, especially from unfamiliar source IPs or outside normal access patterns.

suggestion.title: Detect Cloud Atlas termsrv.dll Modification TTP
suggestion.rationale: Article attributes this specific TTP (termsrv.dll + multi-session RDP) to Cloud Atlas APT Group; this is a rare, high-confidence group signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Create threat-intelligence correlation: termsrv.dll tampering observed in conjunction with multi-session RDP enablement should be tagged as Cloud Atlas activity and escalated accordingly. Cross-reference with known Cloud Atlas C2 infrastructure or credentials if available.

suggestion.title: Detect Privilege Escalation Preceding termsrv.dll Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Modifying System32\termsrv.dll requires SYSTEM/admin privileges; any tampering implies successful privilege escalation. Establish the kill-chain precursor.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on privilege escalation events (UAC bypass, token impersonation, named pipe abuse) occurring 5–30 minutes before termsrv.dll modification. Typical pattern: privilege escalation → DLL tampering → RDP multi-session usage.

suggestion.title: Bulk Account Verification in Financial Services
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'verified bank and fintech mule accounts' being sold; pipeline should detect abnormal account verification velocity and batch verification patterns indicating account takeover or synthetic identity creation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect accounts verified within 24 hours of creation, multiple accounts verified from same device/IP, or verification events clustered by geography. Fintech platforms should flag batch onboarding patterns inconsistent with organic user behavior.

suggestion.title: Rapid Fund Movement from Newly-Verified Accounts
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes 'mule account' model (receive funds, forward to criminals, extract cash); pipeline should detect velocity-based anomaly on newly-verified accounts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when account verified < 3 days prior receives inbound transfer and initiates outbound transfer within 24 hours. Flag accounts with inbound-to-outbound ratio > 95% and time-to-forward < 1 hour as high-confidence mule patterns.

suggestion.title: Impossible Travel / Geographic Inconsistency on Mule Accounts
suggestion.rationale: Account verification locations likely differ from login/transaction locations; article implies mule accounts are sold to geographically dispersed threat actors.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag accounts where account creation and verification originate from one country but initial login/transactions occur in a second country within impossible travel timeframe (e.g., US verification, Brazil login 30 minutes later).

suggestion.title: Account Credential Compromise via Underground Market Indicators
suggestion.rationale: Article describes credentials being sold in Telegram marketplace; pipeline should correlate account compromises with dark-web/telegram credential-sales intelligence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: When threat intelligence indicates account credentials were advertised on Telegram or underground forums, immediately flag that account for 180-day enhanced monitoring including: password change events, recovery attempts, geographic anomalies, and unusual resource access.

suggestion.title: Telegram API / Client Usage from Verified Financial Services Accounts
suggestion.rationale: Cybercriminals coordinate mule networks via Telegram; detection should flag when accounts associated with credential sales show unusual messaging-app usage.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on devices that access verified bank/fintech accounts and simultaneously establish connections to Telegram API, Telegram web clients, or known Telegram proxy IPs. Correlate with time-of-access clustering that suggests coordinated criminal activity.

suggestion.title: Device Code Authentication Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Article states Kali365 'abuses Microsoft's legitimate OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization grant flow' and 'threat actors initiate the device authorization process themselves to generate a code, then trick targets into entering it.' This is the primary attack vector but generated zero detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on device code generation immediately followed by authentication success without password submission. Correlate device code flows from Telegram-sourced phishing campaigns with OAuth token issuance. Flag device code logins from geographies or IP ASNs inconsistent with user baseline.

suggestion.title: Malicious Mailbox Inbox Rule Creation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states attackers 'created malicious inbox rules designed to hide their activity' post-compromise. This is a direct persistence mechanism but produced no detection use case.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on inbox rule creation by accounts showing device code authentication or anomalous OAuth token usage within prior 24 hours. Flag rules forwarding to external domains, creating hidden folders, or using delete/move operations. Correlate with device registration and mailbox access from new IPs.

suggestion.title: Entra Device Registration Following Account Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'attackers also registered new devices in victims' Microsoft environments, further extending their access to the breached network.' No persistence detection generated despite this being post-compromise technique.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor new device registrations to Entra within 2 hours of mailbox rule creation, device code authentication, or OAuth token issuance from unusual IP. Flag registrations from IP addresses geographically impossible from user location. Correlate registration events across multiple user accounts from same source IP (mass compromise indicator).

suggestion.title: OAuth Token Usage Spanning Multiple Cloud Applications
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attackers gaining 'full access to all applications the user normally has access to via their single-sign-on account, including Microsoft 365, Salesforce, or any other cloud SaaS platforms.' No detection for abnormal cross-application OAuth token activity generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when OAuth token generated via device code flow is used to access 3+ distinct cloud applications (Microsoft 365, Salesforce, etc.) within 5 minutes, from IP address different from device code submission. Flag MFA bypass indicated by token usage circumventing re-authentication challenges.

suggestion.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle Session Cookie Capture (Cookie Link Mode)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'Cookie Link' mode that 'proxies victims through attacker-controlled infrastructure that captures authenticated browser sessions, session cookies, and tokens after targets log in and solves MFA challenges.' No session hijacking detection produced.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect MFA challenge completion from one source IP followed by session cookie usage from geographically impossible location or different user agent. Alert on authentication sequences with IP mismatch between credential entry and token usage. Flag user accounts with rapid-fire authentication attempts followed by access from proxy-typical ASNs.

suggestion.title: Phishing Emails Targeting Device Code Portal
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'campaigns primarily targeted Microsoft 365 environments using phishing emails that directed victims to Microsoft's device code login portal.' No email-based initial access detection generated despite being primary infection vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for emails containing links to microsoft.com/devicelogin or homoglyphs thereof, especially from external senders. Flag messages with urgency language ('authorize,' 'confirm code,' 'verify device'). Correlate phishing email receipt with device code authentication attempt from same user account within 2 hours; this is high-fidelity compromise indicator.

suggestion.title: Ghost CMS CVE-2026-26980 Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'Ghost CMS CVE-2026-26980 Exploited to Hijack 700+ Sites.' Pipeline produced zero detection logic for this critical-severity CVE exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Ghost CMS endpoints and admin interfaces for request patterns matching CVE-2026-26980 exploit payloads. Baseline normal Ghost traffic (theme uploads, API calls, admin actions) and alert on anomalous POST/PUT requests to core CMS files or API parameters known vulnerable in this CVE.

suggestion.title: Compromised Ghost Instance Injecting ClickFix Redirects
suggestion.rationale: Article describes sites 'hijacked for ClickFix Attacks' — malware delivery payloads injected into hijacked sites. Pipeline missed the post-compromise persistence and malware distribution phase entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect injected script/iframe tags in HTTP responses from Ghost instances redirecting to malware distribution infrastructure. Alert on Ghost sites serving dynamic ClickFix payloads (fake OS warning popups, browser hijacking redirects). Correlate destination domains against known malware C2 blocklists.

suggestion.title: Ghost CMS Unauthorized Admin User Creation Post-Exploit
suggestion.rationale: Attacker must establish persistence after exploiting CVE-2026-26980 to maintain control of 700+ sites. No persistence detection suggested.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Ghost database audit logs and application logs for creation of new admin users outside change management windows. Alert on ghost_users table INSERT operations with high privilege roles. Cross-reference with approval workflows to identify unauthorized additions.

suggestion.title: Ghost Installation Discovery by Vulnerability Scanners
suggestion.rationale: 700+ sites compromised suggests attacker performed reconnaissance and scanning for vulnerable Ghost instances. Pipeline missed the reconnaissance phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect high-volume requests to common Ghost version detection endpoints (/ghost/api/v3, /ghost/signin, package.json) from single IP/ASN. Flag patterns consistent with vulnerability scanners probing for CVE-2026-26980 presence (specific parameter fuzzing, version fingerprinting requests).

suggestion.title: CDN-Hosted Malicious Payload Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly discusses 'Hackers Abuse Shared CDN Infrastructure'—pipeline did not suggest detection for attacker-controlled content served via legitimate CDN edge nodes. No use case for anomalous payload hosting on high-reputation infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor requests to known CDN domains (Cloudflare, Akamai, etc.) that resolve to suspicious or newly-registered origins, correlate with threat intelligence for malware-hosting patterns, and alert on unusual geographic or file-type distributions from CDN edges.

suggestion.title: Domain Reputation Bypass via Legitimate CDN
suggestion.rationale: Article headline explicitly states 'Bypass Domain Reputation Security Controls'—pipeline produced no detection for reputation-evasion techniques leveraging shared infrastructure trust. Attackers abuse the reputation of the CDN provider to bypass filters.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on phishing or malware URLs that resolve through high-reputation CDN providers but originate from newly-registered or low-reputation subdomains. Cross-reference email gateways for CDN-hosted link delivery with short URL obfuscation.

suggestion.title: Shared Infrastructure IP Reputation Anomalies
suggestion.rationale: Core attack vector is 'Shared CDN Infrastructure'—pipeline missed detection for abuse patterns where attacker content shares infrastructure (IPs, certificates, nameservers) with legitimate content, evading IP-reputation blocks.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor SSL/TLS certificates issued to CDN-shared IPs; flag certificates with mixed legitimate-and-suspicious SANs. Alert on traffic to shared IP ranges when destination subdomains show malware indicators, phishing keywords, or newly-registered domains.

suggestion.title: CDN Provider Abuse Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Attackers must first identify and target specific CDN providers—article discusses infrastructure abuse strategy but pipeline missed initial-access IOC detection for domain reconnaissance targeting CDN-specific subdomains or testing infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect enumeration of CDN-provider subdomains (cdn.*, edge.*, cache.*), queries to known CDN ASNs, and requests to CDN configuration endpoints. Correlate with account creation or public API queries to CDN provider management consoles.

suggestion.title: Suspicious SSH-Like Filenames During Package Installation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes payload hidden 'under SSH-like filename' during package installation; this is the core obfuscation mechanism and a direct detection gap.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor package manager processes (apt, yum, dpkg, rpm) and their spawned children for creation or execution of files with SSH-standard names (ssh, sshd, ssh-agent, ssh-keyscan, ssh-keygen) in atypical locations. Flag if timestamps cluster during package installation and file owners differ from expected package maintainers.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Executable Creation in Package Manager Directories
suggestion.rationale: Payload hidden during package installation suggests malicious binary dropped to package-related paths; article describes this as obfuscation tactic but pipeline generated no file-integrity monitoring UC.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect binary or executable creation in standard package manager cache/staging directories (/var/cache/apt, /var/cache/yum, etc.) with non-standard owners or unexpected execution immediately post-installation. Correlate with package manager process activity.

suggestion.title: Package Installation with Unexpected Network Communication
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attack via package installation likely includes C2 or payload callback; article describes delivery mechanism but pipeline missed network-behavioral detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor child processes spawned by package managers (apt, yum, dpkg) for unexpected outbound network connections to non-repository IPs. Flag if C2 activity correlates with suspicious file creation or masqueraded binary execution.

suggestion.title: Masqueraded SSH Binaries Executed Outside Standard Paths
suggestion.rationale: Article core narrative: legitimate-looking SSH filenames hide malicious payload; detection must surface execution from unexpected locations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect execution of processes named ssh*, sshd*, or ssh-agent from paths outside /usr/bin, /bin, /usr/sbin, /sbin. Correlate with recent package installation activity or unexpected parent processes (e.g., initiated by dpkg or rpm rather than user shell).

suggestion.title: Python Compiled Binary (.pyd) Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title states malware 'ships as .pyd... files'—this is a direct execution vector. Pipeline missed detection of .pyd execution, which is the core attack delivery method.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Python or python.exe spawning .pyd files, or direct execution of .pyd modules (python -m, import statements). Focus on .pyd files from user writable locations, temporary directories, or downloaded files.

suggestion.title: Linux Shared Object (.so) Suspicious Loading Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies malware ships as '.so files' for Linux—no detection logic provided. Should alert on suspicious .so loading, LD_PRELOAD injection, and dynamic linker abuse.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on LD_PRELOAD environment variable set before process execution, dlopen() calls loading .so from /tmp, /dev/shm, or user home directories, and .so files in non-standard library paths with recent modification times.

suggestion.title: Script-to-Binary Evasion Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article headline emphasizes evasion: 'to Evade Script Detection.' No detection case addresses the defense evasion mechanism—compiled binaries bypassing script analysis.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate indicators of legitimate tool (Python, Ruby, Node) execution with sudden appearance of compiled binaries (.pyd, .so, .dll) in script directories or temp paths. Flag Python/Perl/Node processes that do not invoke any .py/.pl/.js files but execute compiled artifacts.

suggestion.title: InvisibleFerret Malware Name/Hash IOC Lookup
suggestion.rationale: Malware family name 'InvisibleFerret' is stated in article title but extracted as zero IOCs. Should create hunting rule for malware family indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: If article supplies sample hashes, domains, or C2 IPs associated with InvisibleFerret, hunt for those in file execution, DNS requests, and network connections. Without full article text, confirm malware name and check VirusTotal, MISP, and threat intel feeds for correlated IOCs.

suggestion.title: Uncommon Python/Library Execution from Non-Standard Paths
suggestion.rationale: Compiled Python modules (.pyd) typically reside in site-packages; unusual paths indicate staging or evasion. Article's evasion focus suggests compiled binaries in anomalous locations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when Python interpreter loads .pyd modules from directories other than %PYTHONPATH%, APPDATA, Program Files, or standard library locations. Cross-reference with file download history and user behavior.

suggestion.title: Compiled Module Injection via Import Hooking
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates .pyd/.so are used to avoid detection—likely loaded dynamically. Detection gap for import hooks, sys.meta_path manipulation, or __import__ override.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Python processes that modify sys.meta_path, sys.path, or hook __import__. Alert on dynamic compilation or ctypes.CDLL calls loading unsigned .so/.dll files. Correlate with environment variable tampering (LD_LIBRARY_PATH, PYTHONPATH).

suggestion.title: SEO Search Result with Malicious Redirect or Suspicious Domain
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'SEO poisoning' as the delivery vector—attacker compromises or spoofs search results to redirect to fake installer. Requires detection of search-engine cached results pointing to unexpected infrastructure or domains mimicking legitimate SQL tools.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for DNS queries or web requests to domains with SQL-related keywords (sqlserver, sql-developer, sqlstudio, etc.) that resolve to non-Microsoft or non-legitimate vendor infrastructure. Correlate with browser history or proxy logs during research sessions. Alert on HTTP 302/301 redirects from search-like pages to installer repositories.

suggestion.title: Fake SQL Developer Installer Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Fake SQL Developer Malware Installer'—attackers bundle malware in an MSI, EXE, or setup binary disguised as legitimate SQL tooling (SQL Server Management Studio, SQL Developer, etc.). Detection must catch execution of unsigned or suspicious installers claiming to be database tools.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of installer processes (MSI, NSIS, InnoSetup, etc.) with display names or file descriptions containing 'SQL', 'Database', 'Developer' if unsigned or signed by unknown publishers. Combine with suspicious child processes (powershell, cmd, regsvr32, rundll32) spawned during or immediately after install completion.

suggestion.title: Persistence or Elevation via SQL Installer Post-Execution Behavior
suggestion.rationale: Fake installers often plant backdoors or add scheduled tasks after initial execution. Article implies malware payload delivery; detection must capture post-install persistence mechanisms typical of APT droppers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for scheduled tasks, registry run keys, or Windows services created by installer processes or child processes spawned by SQL tools. Alert if installer creates named pipes, registry persistence, or spawns unsigned DLLs from temp or appdata folders. Correlate with network callbacks to non-standard C2 ports.

suggestion.title: SQL Developer Targeting in Initial Access Campaigns
suggestion.rationale: Article specifically targets developers via SEO—implies reconnaissance of developer behavior and job titles. Detection should capture anomalous database-tool downloads from non-corporate networks or by users with no legitimate database role.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag downloads of SQL or database admin tools (SQL Server, Oracle Developer, pgAdmin, etc.) from external sources or package mirrors if the downloading user is not in database admin or DBA groups. Correlate with web proxy logs showing suspicious search patterns (e.g., 'SQL Server download', 'free SQL tools').

suggestion.title: Domain Registration or Typosquatting of SQL Vendor Domains
suggestion.rationale: SEO poisoning campaigns typically rely on registered domains spoofing legitimate vendors (e.g., sql-developer.com vs sqlserver.dev vs microsoft-sql.net). Threat hunt should identify attacker-controlled infrastructure mimicking vendor branding.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor WHOIS, passive DNS, and certificate logs for newly registered domains with SQL, database, or developer keywords. Alert on domains with similar-looking names to Microsoft, Oracle, IBM, or open-source database projects. Correlate with malware samples, malicious IP ASNs, or bulletproof hosting providers known to host malware droppers.

suggestion.title: Installer Signed with Stolen or Suspicious Certificates
suggestion.rationale: Advanced malware installers often leverage code-signing bypass or stolen certificates to evade detection. If the fake SQL installer is signed, this should be flagged as unusual or suspicious cert issuance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on executables with display names or descriptions referencing SQL/database tools but signed by certificate authorities or entities unrelated to major database vendors (Microsoft, Oracle, Jetbrains, etc.). Flag code-signing certificate issuance to previously unknown entities in WHOIS or CT logs within 30 days of malware sample first-seen date.

suggestion.title: KnowledgeDeliver LMS Zero-Day Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'KnowledgeDeliver LMS Zero-Day Exploited' as the attack vector. Pipeline failed to generate initial-access detection despite explicit vulnerability reference in title.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for POST/GET requests to KnowledgeDeliver LMS endpoints exhibiting encoding anomalies, multi-stage payloads, or parameter injection patterns. Alert on requests from external IPs to admin, upload, or lesson management paths. Baseline benign LMS activity and flag deviations.

suggestion.title: BLUEBEAM Web Shell File Creation in Web Root
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'BLUEBEAM Web Shell' deployment. Pipeline should detect web shell file creation in web-accessible directories during or after exploit.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on file creation in web root directories (e.g., /var/www/html, C:\inetpub\wwwroot) with executable extensions (.php, .asp, .jsp, .jspx) created shortly after suspicious HTTP activity. Flag files named with shell-like patterns (cmd, shell, admin, upload, gallery).

suggestion.title: Web Shell Process Execution from Web Server Context
suggestion.rationale: Deployed web shell enables command execution. Pipeline missed detection for cmd.exe/powershell spawned from w3wp.exe or apache parent processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, or sh spawned by web server processes (w3wp.exe, apache2, nginx, httpd). Flag parent-child relationships where script interpreter is child of web service. Correlate with web shell file creation events.

suggestion.title: Memory-Only RAT Execution without Disk Staging
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly mentions 'memory-only RAT'—this is a core evasion technique that should trigger detection UCs for process memory analysis and shellcode injection patterns, but pipeline produced no detection logic for it.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Memory-only malware execution typically involves process injection into legitimate executables without corresponding disk writes. Detection should correlate process creation (e.g., rundll32, svchost) with memory-mapped I/O operations and absence of child process file creation, combined with suspicious parent-child chains and unsigned in-memory code execution patterns.

suggestion.title: Lazarus C2 Communication Pattern Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states RemotePE is deployed 'against financial firms'—implies C2 communication occurs, but pipeline generated no network-based UCs for command-and-control detection or beaconing patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Lazarus historically uses DGA, DNS tunneling, and encrypted C2 channels. Detection should flag unusual DNS query patterns from financial sector machines (especially to newly-registered domains), outbound connections to rare/suspicious IPs, and anomalous protocol usage on standard ports masquerading as HTTPS.

suggestion.title: Phishing/Initial Access for Financial Sector Targeting
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies financial and crypto firms as targets but pipeline produced no initial-access UCs. Historical Lazarus attacks on finance use spear-phishing and watering holes; article title does not specify delivery mechanism, indicating pipeline should have flagged this gap.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for spear-phishing indicators targeting financial institutions: emails with finance-themed subject lines sent to trading/treasury roles, macro-enabled documents from unusual origins, or links to credential harvesting sites. Cross-correlate with employee security awareness data to identify high-risk clicks on Lazarus-attributed domains.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement Detection in Financial Networks
suggestion.rationale: Memory-only RAT deployment into financial firms suggests lateral movement to critical systems (trading platforms, payment servers); article title establishes scope but pipeline generated zero lateral-movement detection logic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Within financial networks, monitor for credential reuse across segmented systems, unusual RDP/WinRM traffic between workstations and critical servers, NTLM relay attacks, and administrative shares access from non-privileged user contexts. Flag rapid sequential lateral-movement attempts indicating post-exploitation reconnaissance.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration to Cryptocurrency Wallets/Mixers
suggestion.rationale: Title mentions 'crypto firms' as targets; article should describe exfiltration of keys, balances, or transaction data, but pipeline produced zero exfiltration/impact UCs despite this being Lazarus's proven motivation (financial theft).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for bulk data exfiltration to known cryptocurrency exchanges, mixing services, or anonymization infrastructure. Flag archive creation (7z, rar) on crypto exchange servers followed by SFTP/HTTPS transfers to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Cross-reference against threat feeds for known Lazarus exfiltration nodes and blockchain transaction monitoring where possible.

suggestion.title: RemotePE-Specific File Indicators and Hashing
suggestion.rationale: RemotePE is named explicitly in the title, but pipeline extracted zero IOCs (empty {}). Should minimally include file hashes, C2 domains, or IP indicators associated with RemotePE samples described in the article.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish file hash baselines for RemotePE variants (SHA256, SSDEEP) and alert on execution. Monitor for suspicious .NET/C# runtime invocation (csc.exe, vbc.exe) from unexpected parents, and in-memory .NET assembly loading without corresponding on-disk compiled assemblies (CLR profiling hooks).
