suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for generated Python files containing specific patterns: @app.route('/chat'), @app.route('/agents'), or Flask boilerplate created by the generate_api_server_code function. Watch for new .py files in temp dirs or deployment paths shortly after `praisonai deploy` execution.

suggestion.title: YAML Deployment Config Inspection (Vulnerable Settings)
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'recommended sample YAML' triggers the vulnerability. UC_9_3 hunts the command, but no UC validates the YAML config for insecure port/bind/auth settings before deployment.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect creation or modification of YAML files containing port: 8005, host: 0.0.0.0, or authentication: disabled/false in the context of praisonai deployments. Pair with process execution of `praisonai deploy` within minutes.

suggestion.title: Default Flask Port 8005 Process Ownership Anomaly
suggestion.rationale: UC_9_4 hunts network inbound, but doesn't correlate process ownership. If a non-service account (e.g., user shell, cron, CI/CD pipeline) spawns the Flask listener, it's a configuration anomaly worth flagging ahead of exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate listening processes on 8005 with initiating process account and parent. Flag if initiated by developer accounts, ad-hoc Python shells, or non-service accounts. Expected: service account or deployment automation; suspicious: interactive user, CI/CD agent, or shell session.

suggestion.title: Forged JWT Token Usage — Multiple User Identities from Single Source
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'allowing token forgery for any user when PLATFORM_ENV is unset'. Detection should target successful authentication events presenting different user principals from the same source IP in rapid succession, which indicates token forgery post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for authentication success events (HTTP 200 on /auth/me or /workspaces/ endpoints) from a single IP address where the authenticated User/Principal changes multiple times within a short window (e.g., 5+ distinct users in 10 minutes). Token forgery bypasses normal session management; rapid user-switching is the fingerprint.

suggestion.title: Hardcoded JWT Secret Detection — Process or Environment Exposure
suggestion.rationale: Article describes: 'JWT signing secret defaults to the hardcoded literal "dev-secret-change-me"'. Forensic detection should flag any process, config file, or log output containing the known hardcoded secret, which would confirm exploitation or misconfiguration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for string 'dev-secret-change-me' or 'dev-secret-change' in process command lines, environment variable dumps, configuration files (*.env, *.json, *.yaml in /etc/praisonai* or app directories), and memory dumps. Any match indicates either a vulnerable default deployment or an attacker who extracted the secret.

suggestion.title: PLATFORM_ENV Environment Exploitation — Absence or Explicit 'dev' Override
suggestion.rationale: Article core flaw: 'A safety check exists but only fires when PLATFORM_ENV != "dev"; the default value of PLATFORM_ENV is "dev"'. Detection should hunt for deployments or runtime invocations where PLATFORM_ENV is explicitly set to 'dev' in production network segments, or missing entirely on production-labeled hosts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for praisonai_platform processes on production/staging-classified hosts where PLATFORM_ENV env var is either absent (relying on dangerous default) or explicitly set to 'dev'. Cross-reference process owner and network location; mismatches (prod network, dev config) indicate misconfiguration or intentional exploitation.

suggestion.title: JWT Token Validation Bypass — Failed auth followed by API success
suggestion.rationale: Article impact: 'allowing token forgery for any user when PLATFORM_ENV is unset'. If attackers craft tokens directly, they may bypass initial auth checks but succeed at API endpoints. Detect HTTP 401→403 (auth fail/forbidden) followed immediately by HTTP 200 (success) on /workspaces or /auth/me with identical or suspicious token signatures.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate HTTP response codes: a source making requests that receive 401 (Unauthorized) or 403 (Forbidden), then immediately switching to 200 OK responses on the same API endpoints without a re-authentication event, suggests token forgery or validation bypass in progress.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Workspace role escalation via API audit logs (successful role-change in application logs)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states the vulnerability is in the `PATCH /workspaces/{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}` endpoint. Application-layer audit logs will show the role-change event. Detection pipeline did not suggest hunting application audit logs at all, only network/endpoint layers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor application audit logs for workspace member role changes (especially escalations to 'owner' or 'admin'). Correlate with originating user_id and timestamp. Flag role changes initiated by non-owner accounts or by accounts that did not previously have admin rights in the workspace.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Access to data endpoints immediately following unauthorized role escalation
suggestion.rationale: After escalating privileges, an attacker would enumerate workspace data they now have access to. Article mentions T1213/T1530 as consequences. No UC detects the data-access phase post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After detecting a successful role-escalation PATCH (200/204 response), monitor for GET requests to workspace data endpoints from the same user within 5–30 minutes. Flag if the user accesses resources they could not access before the role change (infer from historical baseline).

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Authorization check bypass — 403 escalation to 200 on member-update endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article states the endpoint is gated by `require_workspace_member(workspace_id)` with `min_role='member'`, never overridden. A sophisticated attacker might first attempt the request and receive 403/401, then escalate. No UC detects this pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for a sequence: HTTP 403/401 response on PATCH /workspaces/*/members/* followed by a 200/204 response on the same endpoint from the same source IP and user within 60 seconds. This suggests reconnaissance followed by successful exploitation.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Bulk workspace member role changes by a single user in short time window
suggestion.rationale: Attack might involve promoting multiple accounts (confederates) to owner in rapid succession. No UC detects bulk role-change activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for a single user initiating PATCH requests to modify member roles on 3+ distinct user_ids within 10 minutes. Flag especially if targeted users are escalated to owner/admin role.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Workspace member role escalation + immediate deactivation of legitimate admin
suggestion.rationale: A more sophisticated attack flow: attacker promotes self, then removes or demotes the legitimate workspace owner to disable recovery. This is a variation of UC_4_3 but framed as disable-owner rather than just demotion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect a sequence: PATCH request that escalates one user to owner, followed within 30 minutes by a PATCH request that demotes or deactivates a different user who was previously an owner (check baseline). Flag if the first PATCH user and the demoted user differ.

suggestion.title: AI Coding Tool Configuration Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes GitHub Copilot integration and Snyk scanning as critical security controls: 'developers could generate code, receive security findings immediately.' Compromise of these integrations would bypass core controls. No existing detection assumes threat actor targeting AI tool configs themselves.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unauthorized changes to GitHub Copilot settings, Snyk integration auth tokens, or pre-commit hook scripts. Detect lateral movement into developer machine CI/CD tool configs. Alert on revocation/reinstall of security scanning tools by non-admin users.

suggestion.title: Malicious Dependency Injection via AI Output
suggestion.rationale: Article describes AI-generated code flowing directly into commits via custom pre-commit hooks: 'developers could generate code...and apply fixes in real time before code was ever committed.' If AI tool or its supply chain is compromised, malicious dependencies bypass human review.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect novel or typosquatted dependencies introduced in commits that pass pre-commit scanning. Alert on dependencies added by junior developers at unusual times. Correlate with known compromise of popular packages; monitor for duplicate or near-identical dependency names.

suggestion.title: Pre-Commit Hook Bypass or Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Article highlights custom pre-commit hooks as a core security control: 'forces the research right there while it's in front of you.' Attackers with repo access would disable or modify hooks to skip scanning. No detection for hook deletion/modification.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor .git/hooks directory for unauthorized deletions, permission changes, or overwrite. Alert on commits that disable or uninstall security scanning tools. Detect when pre-commit output is suppressed or logs are deleted.

suggestion.title: Exfiltration via AI Tool Logs or Generated Code
suggestion.rationale: Article notes developers use AI tools within GitHub for code generation: 'GitHub Copilot matured, Brendan saw a clear shift. Today, AI has become a core part.' AI tools may log sensitive context or generated code to external services; compromise could exfiltrate proprietary algorithms.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor network traffic from developer machines to non-standard GitHub or Copilot endpoints. Alert on unusual volumes of data to Microsoft/GitHub services during off-hours. Detect if .copilot config or API keys are read by unexpected processes.

suggestion.title: LinkedIn Spearphishing Link Click Followed by macOS Process Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly describes 'LinkedIn Social Engineering to Deploy Custom macOS Malware.' Pipeline generated zero initial-access or execution detections despite clear phishing vector and payload deployment pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: User clicks malicious link from LinkedIn message or profile, downloads executable disguised as innocuous file. Subsequent process execution from ~/Downloads or /tmp with suspicious command-line arguments (script interpreters, reverse shells, package installation). Look for Python/Bash execution spawned by browser or Archive Utility within 2 minutes of suspicious network activity.

suggestion.title: Suspicious macOS Application Execution from Atypical Paths
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'custom macOS malware' but pipeline captured no execution indicators. Malware deployed via social engineering typically executes from user-writable directories or masquerades as legitimate app.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for executable or script execution from ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop, /tmp, or /var/tmp on macOS. Flag processes spawning child processes with network connectivity (curl, nc, python -m socket) within seconds of user interaction. Custom malware often lacks valid code signatures.

suggestion.title: LinkedIn Profile Reconnaissance for Targeting
suggestion.rationale: Social engineering attack presupposes reconnaissance. Article states actor uses LinkedIn as vector but pipeline captured no discovery/reconnaissance indicators despite this being prerequisite to phishing success.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate LinkedIn API calls or web requests to LinkedIn profile pages of security/sysadmin personnel with subsequent phishing delivery. Profile view patterns (many views from single IP over short window) followed by connection requests and message delivery may signal coordinated social engineering campaign.

suggestion.title: VS Code Tunnels Abuse for C2
suggestion.rationale: Article title states Kimsuky 'Expands Arsenal with VS Code Tunnels'—direct indication of malicious tunnel infrastructure abuse for command and control that pipeline did not surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for VS Code Tunnel daemon processes establishing persistent outbound connections, tunnel ID registration to external relay servers, and VS Code spawning child processes with network-forwarding arguments. Alert on tunnel process creation by non-developer accounts.

suggestion.title: HelloDoor Malware Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title lists 'HelloDoor' as part of Kimsuky's expanded toolkit; pipeline did not propose any detection coverage for this malware family.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HelloDoor process name/hash execution, PowerShell script block logs containing HelloDoor-related download-and-execute patterns, and file system artifacts matching HelloDoor staging directories or installer filenames.

suggestion.title: HTTPSpy HTTPS Exfiltration Detection
suggestion.rationale: Title names HTTPSpy as newly deployed capability; pipeline omitted detection for this tool's HTTPS data exfiltration and reconnaissance command retrieval patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTPS traffic with HTTPSpy user-agent signatures or atypical HTTPS POST patterns to known/suspected Kimsuky C2 infrastructure. Monitor for encrypted tunnel traffic with anomalous byte patterns or timing indicative of exfiltration over HTTP/HTTPS.

suggestion.title: Kimsuky Lateral Movement via Tunnel Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates toolkit expansion for offensive capability; pipeline failed to propose detection for lateral movement abuse of the new tunneling tools.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for repeated tunnel endpoint connections between internal systems, unusual RDP or SSH proxying through VS Code Tunnel relay infrastructure, and lateral movement attempting to establish new tunnel listeners on compromised hosts.

suggestion.title: Kimsuky Malware Family Hash/Signature Coverage
suggestion.rationale: Actor name 'Kimsuky' appears in title but pipeline did not map to known Kimsuky-attributed file hashes, YARA signatures, or TTPs (e.g., WMI execution, scheduled task abuse).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference executable hashes and domains against Kimsuky malware repositories. Alert on Kimsuky-attributed TTPs: WMI command-line execution, scheduled task creation for persistence, and registry modifications matching known Kimsuky malware families.

suggestion.title: Suspicious NuGet Package Installation from Public Repository
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly describes 'malicious NuGet package.' Pipeline missed initial-access vector—likely typosquatting or dependency-confusion attack on legitimate Sicoob SDK.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor nuget.exe and dotnet CLI restore/install activity for fetches of packages matching known SDKs with name variants or unusual source configurations. Alert on installation of packages with similar names to legitimate banking/fintech libraries (typosquatting indicators). Baseline legitimate SDK versions and flag any deviation from pinned versions in internal projects.

suggestion.title: Credential Exfiltration from Banking Software Context
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'exfiltrates banking passwords'; pipeline missed credential-access and exfiltration detections. Attack specifically targets Sicoob integration layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect LSASS access, credential store enumeration (CredEnumerate, CredRead Win32 API), or registry queries for banking software config/password storage from .NET runtime processes. Alert on process chains where NuGet or dependency resolution precedes credential-dumping activity by <1 hour. Monitor for in-memory credential extraction patterns via .NET reflection or P/Invoke.

suggestion.title: .NET Assembly Execution from Package Cache with Malicious Behavior
suggestion.rationale: Malicious code embedded in NuGet package executes during dependency resolution or assembly load. Pipeline missed execution-phase detection specific to .NET supply-chain attacks.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child processes or unsigned assembly loads originating from NuGet cache directory (%USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages). Flag .NET compiler/runtime processes (csc.exe, dotnet.exe, msbuild.exe) spawning unexpected child processes. Correlate assembly load events with subsequent network connections or file writes to credential paths.

suggestion.title: C2 Communication from .NET Process with Exfiltrated Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Article describes password exfiltration; pipeline missed exfiltration-phase detection. Malware communicates with attacker infrastructure to transmit stolen banking credentials.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound TLS connections from .NET runtime processes to non-whitelisted destinations (especially non-banking infrastructure). Alert on POST/PUT traffic from .NET processes carrying base64-encoded or compressed payloads (credential blobs). Correlate credential-access event timestamps with outbound network connections within 5-minute window.

suggestion.title: Anomalous NuGet Source Configuration or Repository Access
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attack may involve malicious NuGet source added to project or substitution of legitimate source. Pipeline did not capture repo-level attack detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor changes to NuGet.Config files (additions of non-standard sources, source reordering). Alert on restore operations against internal/private feeds followed by installation from external feeds (priority inversion). Flag projects with 'Allow Prerelease' or disabled signature verification settings.

suggestion.title: Persistence via Malicious NuGet Dependency in Project File
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates SDK replacement; attackers typically persist through project dependencies to re-infect on rebuild. Pipeline missed persistence-phase detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor .csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj files for package references to suspicious package names or versions. Alert on package version downgrades or switches to less-stable versions (pre-release tags). Track projects that depend on packages with high edit/upload frequency (possible attacker re-uploads after deletion/restoration).

suggestion.title: Malicious NuGet/npm Package Installation with Credential Access
suggestion.rationale: Article core claim: 'Malicious Sicoob NuGet Steals Banking Credentials' — packages must be detected during installation, then correlated with subsequent credential-system access (Windows Credential Manager, SAM, cloud credential files).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate NuGet.exe or npm.exe process execution with child processes accessing credential stores (Windows Credential Manager registry hives, .aws/credentials, ~/.azure/*, .gcp/*). Alert on 'Sicoob' or known-malicious package installation followed by Credential Manager enumeration or cloud CLI credential reads.

suggestion.title: Cloud Secret Enumeration and Exfiltration from Package Execution Context
suggestion.rationale: Article subtitle explicitly states npm packages 'Target Cloud Secrets' — packages installed from untrusted sources should never enumerate environment variables like AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, or GCP credentials.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor processes spawned from NuGet/npm installation directories for environment variable reads matching cloud secret patterns (AWS_*, AZURE_*, GCP_*, DB_*). Detect unexpected cloud API calls (AssumeRole, ListSecrets, GetSecretValue) from compute instances immediately post-package-install. Flag data staging in temp directories followed by exfiltration.

suggestion.title: Banking Credential Theft via Infostealer Patterns in Package Code
suggestion.rationale: Article states malicious package 'Steals Banking Credentials' — code within package should be scanned for credentials scraping (browser storage, password manager access), credential regex patterns, or banking API interactions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect package installation processes accessing Chrome/Edge credential stores, Firefox profile directories, or Windows Credential Manager. Alert on process handles to browsers/password managers from package-spawned child processes. Flag network traffic from package processes to banking or third-party credential lookup services.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Attack Detection: Malicious Package Installation via Package Managers
suggestion.rationale: Attack vector is explicitly malicious packages in NuGet and npm registries — article title 'Malicious Sicoob NuGet' and 'npm Packages'. Baseline detection must flag any installation of packages on known-malicious or suspicious similarity list.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain allowlist/denylist of package names. Trigger detection on installation via NuGet.exe, dotnet restore, npm install, yarn of flagged packages like 'Sicoob' or typosquatting variants. Inspect package.json, .csproj, .nuspec files during CI/CD pipelines for malicious dependencies. Alert on package version downgrades or unexpected package source changes.

suggestion.title: Post-Installation Persistence via Scheduled Tasks or Services from Package Directories
suggestion.rationale: Malicious packages commonly establish persistence mechanisms after initial execution. Look for suspicious service or scheduled task creation spawned from package installation processes or directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for sc.exe, New-Service, or schtasks.exe spawned from NuGet/npm installation directories or package processes. Alert on persistence mechanisms (services, scheduled tasks, registry boot-start) with binary paths pointing to package directories. Flag unusual system process parents originating from TEMP or AppData package paths.

suggestion.title: Data Staging and Encoding Patterns for Credential Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Title states credentials are stolen — expect staging in temp directories, Base64/encoding, or compression before transmission. 'Steals Banking Credentials' implies collection then exfiltration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect file writes to %TEMP% or %AppData% from package-spawned processes containing Base64-encoded strings, JSON with 'password'/'secret'/'key' fields, or PII regex matches (credit card, SSN). Flag compression (zip, rar, 7z) of credential files from package contexts. Monitor for files containing banking domain names or cloud provider credential markers.

suggestion.title: GREYVIBE AI-Powered Command Injection Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly mentions 'AI-powered cyberattacks'—suggests LLM-assisted exploitation or command generation. No use case generated despite this attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for command-line invocations with unusual patterns characteristic of LLM-generated payloads (e.g., high token entropy, unusual syntax orders, repeated function calls with minor variations). Correlate with network IOCs once article content is available.

suggestion.title: Ukraine-Targeting C2 Beaconing
suggestion.rationale: Title confirms Ukrainian targets; article must contain C2 infrastructure details or IP ranges. No kill-chain phase for C2 was extracted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on outbound connections from Ukrainian networks to known GREYVIBE C2 infrastructure. Requires IOC extraction from full article to populate allowlists. Flag unusual DNS queries with timing patterns consistent with beaconing.

suggestion.title: GREYVIBE Initial Access via Phishing or Watering Hole
suggestion.rationale: Title establishes targeting but does not specify attack vector; article body should document initial compromise method (phishing, exploit, supply chain). No initial_access phase detected.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: If phishing: flag emails with malicious attachments or URLs to GREYVIBE infrastructure. If web-based: monitor for exploitation attempts against known CVEs attributed to campaign. Requires article specifics to refine.

suggestion.title: Windows Scheduled Task Creation with Ransomware Command Line Indicators
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Ransomware Uses SYSTEM Scheduled Task' as the delivery mechanism. This is the primary execution vector — no detection UC generated despite being the attack's core TTPs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor schtasks.exe /create executed with elevated privileges, creating tasks in SYSTEM context. Flag suspicious runlevels (RunLevel=Highest), executable paths in temp/appdata, immediate scheduling or scheduled runs post-compromise, and tasks deleted shortly after creation.

suggestion.title: High-Volume File Encryption by SYSTEM-Context Process
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'encrypt local drives with elevated privileges' — ransomware files are encrypted by processes running as SYSTEM. Expected log avalanche of file-write, file-encryption, or sequential modification events across multiple directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect high-speed bulk file modifications by processes running as SYSTEM (AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) across user directories. Flag sequential writes to files with identical or novel extensions, cryptographic patterns in file content, or >1000 file modifications within 5-minute windows.

suggestion.title: Scheduled Task Spawn of Encryption Process
suggestion.rationale: The attack chain requires scheduled task invocation → encryption subprocess. Correlation between task creation/execution and child encryption process is a direct indicator of this attack pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate schtasks.exe process creation with subsequent child processes showing file encryption behavior (high-frequency file I/O, bulk writes, cryptographic library calls). Look for temporal clustering within 60 seconds and privilege elevation from user context to SYSTEM.

suggestion.title: Post-Encryption Ransom Note Creation
suggestion.rationale: Ransomware impacts are evidenced by artifact creation: ransom notes with predictable names and locations. Article implies 'encrypted local drives' → ransom notes deposited.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for creation of common ransom note filenames (README.txt, RECOVERY.html, HELP_YOUR_FILES.txt, RESTORE_FILES.txt) in bulk across directories. Flag file creation by ransomware-associated processes or file writes containing ransom demand keywords.

suggestion.title: Scheduled Task Deletion or Modification Post-Encryption
suggestion.rationale: Sophisticated ransomware cleans up scheduled tasks post-execution to evade forensics, or repurposes them for persistence. Article implies task-driven attack — post-encryption task state changes are evasion or persistence indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor schtasks.exe /delete or /change commands clustering temporally with encryption activity. Watch registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache for deletion events. Flag scheduled task re-creation or modification with new persistence-oriented triggers.

suggestion.title: Anomalous API Calls to ChatGPT/Gemini Endpoints from Enterprise Identity
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states hackers 'leverage ChatGPT and Google Gemini'—this is the attack vector. Pipeline extracted zero detections for AI service abuse despite clear methodology statement.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on high-volume, geo-anomalous, or off-hours API calls to OpenAI/Google Gemini endpoints from compromised user credentials. Correlate with credential-access indicators. Watch for token reuse across multiple source IPs or non-standard request patterns (batch requests, malware development keywords in logged prompts).

suggestion.title: Phishing Content Generated via Compromised AI Service Tokens
suggestion.rationale: If GREYVIBE is leveraging ChatGPT/Gemini, phishing content generation is the obvious attack path. Pipeline missed detection for synthetic phishing indicators paired with enterprise AI API usage.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect emails with linguistic markers of LLM generation (unusual token-choice patterns, excessive hypercorrection, structural formatting consistent with AI output) sent from accounts with recent AI API access. Correlate mass phishing campaigns with token usage spikes.

suggestion.title: Malware Development Prompts Sent to AI Services
suggestion.rationale: Threat actors using ChatGPT/Gemini to develop malware is implied by 'fuel cyberattacks.' Pipeline produced no detection for prompts containing shellcode, obfuscation, or malware-development keywords.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor AI service API logs (via audit or CASB) for prompts requesting shellcode generation, obfuscation techniques, persistence mechanisms, or credential-exfiltration code. Flag accounts with repeated malware-development assistance requests.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting via AI-Generated Social-Engineering Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: No detection for AI-assisted credential harvesting campaigns. 'Fuel cyberattacks' implies multi-stage attack; credential access is the obvious next phase after phishing generation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate phishing campaigns (with LLM markers) that successfully redirect users to credential-harvest pages with OAuth or MFA-bypass attempts. Monitor for unusual login patterns post-phishing.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Install with Reconnaissance Indicators
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 33 malicious npm packages used to 'collect reconnaissance data from developer and build environments.' Pipeline missed UC for detecting install-time behavioral indicators (env var exfil, system info gathering, shell execution during postinstall).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm postinstall / install scripts that spawn child processes (sh, cmd, powershell) immediately after package extraction. Flag calls to system interrogation APIs (uname, whoami, hostname, systeminfo, env) or calls to curl/wget during install phase. Correlate with known malicious package names.

suggestion.title: Dependency Confusion Resolution to Public Registry
suggestion.rationale: Attack vector explicitly 'abuses dependency confusion' — expect package.json or lock file references to public npm packages masquerading as internal scoped packages. Pipeline missed detection for resolution mismatches between declared scope and actual source.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on npm install/ci operations that resolve @internal-namespace/* or similar scoped packages from public registries (npmjs.com) when organization's .npmrc or config specifies an internal registry. Cross-reference resolved package version with internal package database—mismatches indicate confusion attack.

suggestion.title: Malicious npm Package Exfiltration of Developer Environment Variables
suggestion.rationale: Article states packages 'profile developer environments'—likely targeting NODE_ENV, CI environment variables, git credentials, AWS keys, etc. during install. Pipeline failed to suggest detection for env var access during package lifecycle.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on npm package postinstall scripts that read process.env object and send it to external URL (via curl, axios, fetch). Flag child processes spawned by npm with file descriptors opened to ~/.ssh, ~/.aws/credentials, .git/config, or environment variable enumeration followed by network egress.

suggestion.title: npm Package C2 Callback with Developer Machine Telemetry
suggestion.rationale: Reconnaissance focus implies C2 callback or data exfil phase. Article mentions 'observed tradecraft' suggesting callback infrastructure—pipeline did not surface expected domains, IPs, or HTTP patterns for data exfil.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor DNS queries and HTTP/HTTPS connections initiated by npm processes (node.exe, npm.cmd) pointing to newly registered or reputation-unknown domains. Flag connections encoding system info in User-Agent, POST body, or query parameters (e.g. machine_id=, os=, env=). Correlate with malicious package names or known C2 IOCs.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Global Package Installation with System Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Dependency confusion attacks may use `-g` flag to install globally. If packages add shell hooks or init scripts, they could achieve persistence. Article mentions 'profile developer environments'—potential for install-time backdoors. Pipeline missed persistence detection UC.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on npm install -g commands for unknown or suspicious packages. Flag postinstall scripts that write to ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, ~/.bash_profile, npm prefix bin, or /usr/local/bin. Monitor for subsequent shell initialization that sources injected files.

suggestion.title: Detection of Known Malicious npm Package Names in Lock Files
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline output contains zero IOCs—no package names, hashes, or checksums from the 33 identified packages. Yara/SIEM rule for hash or name matching is absent. This is the most basic detection and was completely omitted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml for hardcoded indicators (malicious package names, versions, checksums) from threat intel feeds or security advisories. Alert on any match in dev, CI, or build environments. Cross-reference with npm audit results.

suggestion.title: GlobalProtect Portal Authentication Bypass Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'Under Active Exploitation'—pipeline must map initial access patterns. CVE-2026-0257 targets authentication layer; detection hypothesis requires unusual portal access and failed/malformed auth sequences.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for repeated POST requests to /ssl-vpn/login.esp or /global-protect/portal.cgi with missing/malformed session tokens, non-standard User-Agent strings, or payloads exceeding normal parameter size. Flag 401/403 bursts followed by successful 200 without valid pre-auth session state.

suggestion.title: Post-Bypass Credential Dumping from VPN Gateway
suggestion.rationale: Auth bypass naturally precedes credential theft from compromised appliance. Article's 'active exploitation' context implies attackers achieve system-level access to gateway.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect suspicious file access on PAN-OS gateway targeting /opt/panvpn, /etc/passwd, or certificate stores. Monitor for process execution of credential dumping tools (mimikatz, hashcat) spawned from web service context or unusual privilege escalations to root.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement via Compromised VPN Session
suggestion.rationale: GlobalProtect is external-facing remote access; auth bypass grants attacker trusted network position. Article's 'active exploitation' indicates post-lateral-move discovery/scanning activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect RDP/SSH/WinRM connections originating from GlobalProtect gateway IP to internal assets. Monitor for SMB enumeration (\\\\<ip>\\c$), DNS queries for internal service discovery, and unusual process execution (PsExec, WMI) from VPN source IPs.

suggestion.title: Command and Control Exfiltration via VPN Tunnel
suggestion.rationale: Bypassed auth enables attacker to abuse VPN as trusted C2 channel. Article title 'active exploitation' directly implies attackers maintain persistent remote access.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for encrypted tunneling protocols (SSH, VPN-in-VPN, DNS-over-HTTPS) established through GlobalProtect to external C2 endpoints. Detect beaconing patterns from internal hosts through VPN gateway with periodic callbacks to suspicious IPs/domains.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-39987 Marimo RCE Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states 'Attackers Use LLM Agent for Post-Exploitation After Marimo CVE-2026-39987 Exploit' — indicates known vulnerability exploitation as initial access. Pipeline extracted zero IOCs and zero kill-chain despite this being the attack entry point.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTP requests to Marimo instances matching known CVE-2026-39987 exploitation signatures. Monitor for request patterns typical of RCE probing (POST to eval/exec endpoints, payload encoding, unusual parameter names) followed by successful response codes and subsequent unusual subprocess activity.

suggestion.title: LLM Agent Post-Exploitation Execution
suggestion.rationale: Title specifies 'LLM Agent for Post-Exploitation' after initial compromise. This is the primary attack mechanism but zero execution-phase detections were generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for subprocess spawning from Marimo Python processes with characteristics of LLM agent orchestration: variable/high-entropy command arguments, repeated rapid subprocess creation, invocation of scripting interpreters (bash/powershell), or API calls to LLM service endpoints (OpenAI, etc.).

suggestion.title: Detect ChatGPT Summary with Embedded Image URLs from Untrusted Domains
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'auto-fetches those images and surfaces those links as live, clickable elements inside the trusted assistant UI.' Pipeline missed the core observable: Markdown-formatted image URLs pointing to attacker infrastructure within ChatGPT response boundaries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor ChatGPT API responses for Markdown image syntax (![alt](url)) where the domain is flagged as attacker-controlled or newly registered. Correlate with HTTP GET requests for images containing authentication-related headers (User-Agent, Referer, Authorization) to untrusted external endpoints. Baseline legitimate summarization patterns to reduce false positives.

suggestion.title: Identify Prompt Injection Payload in Web Page Summaries
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'bad actor can append a small payload to any web page' and 'LLMs cannot reliably distinguish between legitimate instructions and attacker-supplied content.' Pipeline failed to flag suspicious instruction-like text embedded in summarized content.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on ChatGPT summaries that contain imperative language inconsistent with page content (e.g., 'click this link', 'enter your credentials', 'download this file') when those instructions originate from third-party page markup rather than narrative content. Flag summaries that include raw Markdown commands, inline HTML, or script-like directives.

suggestion.title: Detect Data Exfiltration via HTTP Image Request Headers
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability 'cause[s] it to leak their IP, User-Agent, and Referer details when attacker-hosted images embedded in the page are automatically fetched.' Pipeline missed observable HTTP metadata exfiltration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP GET requests to image-serving endpoints from ChatGPT or browser contexts where Referer headers, User-Agent, and source IP are unintentionally exposed. Establish baseline of legitimate image CDNs and alert on requests to newly-observed or suspicious domains with full header verbosity.

suggestion.title: Detect Permiso Security ChatGPhish Proof-of-Concept Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'Permiso submitted the initial vulnerability report to OpenAI via Bugcrowd on April 29, 2026, and the research was publicly published on May 29, 2026.' Permiso's public PoC and disclosures should be monitored as attack templates.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Permiso Security's ChatGPhish research repository access (GitHub, academic servers), downloads of PoC code, or domains referenced in Permiso's published attack walkthroughs. Flag employees or automated systems downloading or cloning ChatGPhish tooling.

suggestion.title: Alert on Markdown Injection in ChatGPT Web Summary Output
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'chatgpt.com response renderer trusts Markdown links and Markdown image URLs' and surfaces 'formatted alerts, clickable links, and inline images.' Pipeline should have detected Markdown structural anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Markdown syntax in ChatGPT summaries that does not correspond to visible text in the original page summarized. Compare rendered Markdown image/link counts and domains against the source page's actual link structure. Alert on mismatches indicating injected payloads.

suggestion.title: Monitor for Social Engineering Campaigns Leveraging ChatGPhish
suggestion.rationale: Article describes scenario where 'bad actor can append a small payload to any web page that the victim later prompts ChatGPT to summarize.' This presupposes a social engineering campaign to trick users into requesting summaries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor email and messaging for URLs pointing to recently-registered or suspicious domains accompanied by requests to 'summarize this in ChatGPT' or 'ask ChatGPT to analyze this page.' Track phishing campaigns that exploit ChatGPhish as a vector by redirecting victims through legitimate summaries before credential harvesting.

suggestion.title: Google Ad Redirect to ChatGPT Shared Phishing Page
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states threat actors 'use Google ads to direct users searching for ChatGPT to a malicious shared ChatGPT page hosted on chatgpt.com' — this is the initial-access vector and should trigger on ad-referrer traffic to suspicious chatgpt.com/s/ endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for requests to chatgpt.com/s/ or claude.ai artifact URLs arriving from Google Ads referrers or ad-tagged traffic. Flag pages containing 'outage', 'unavailable', or download prompts. Correlate with subsequent downloads from attacker infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Malware Download from Domain Impersonating OpenAI
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers host downloads at 'openew[.]app that impersonates OpenAI's desktop application download portal' and the site 'uses cloaking to display content only to targeted victims' — T1036 masquerading with anti-analysis evasion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect downloads from domains that homograph-attack known vendors (openai, anthropic, openew). Correlate suspicious executable downloads with cloaking-indicators (requests return benign content to scanners but malware to users) and flag for sandboxing.

suggestion.title: VM Detection Commands Executed by Downloaded Malware
suggestion.rationale: Article documents that Windows malware 'executes various commands to determine whether the device is a legitimate computer or a virtual machine' — standard T1497.001 sandbox evasion to avoid detection/analysis.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for execution of wmic, systeminfo, reg query, or Get-WmiObject targeting hypervisor/VM vendor detection (wmic computersystem get manufacturer, Hyper-V registry paths) within seconds of suspicious application downloads. Flag parent processes named for ChatGPT/OpenAI installers.

suggestion.title: Infostealer Distribution via AI Platform Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'earlier campaigns abusing AI platform sharing features have distributed infostealers' and notes Claude Artifacts were abused for ClickFix attacks — AI artifact-sharing is now an established malware delivery channel.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate downloads from openew[.]-like domains with known infostealer behaviors: browser password manager access, Chrome/Firefox session cookie enumeration, registry lookups for stored credentials, C2 beacons to known stealer C2 infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Fake Outage Notice Hosted on Legitimate AI Platform Domain
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'fake outage notice is rendered through ChatGPT itself... published through a shared chatgpt.com/s/ link' with 'Show code' and 'Remix' controls visible — leverages domain reputation to bypass security filters.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outage-themed or application-download-prompting pages served from chatgpt.com/s/ and claude.ai artifact domains. Flag pages with suspicious HTML/CSS attempting to impersonate service status pages or download portals. Block or warn on subsequent navigation to attacker C2 domains.

suggestion.title: Multi-Hop Redirect Chain: Ad → Legitimate Share → Malware Site
suggestion.rationale: Article describes complete chain: Google Ads → chatgpt.com/s/ (legitimate) → openew[.]app (malware). This three-hop pattern is designed to defeat URL reputation checks by routing through trusted platforms.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag redirect chains where an ad platform or search referrer points to a legitimate AI platform share link, which then redirects or prompts download from attacker domain. Monitor referrer chains and flag when trusted-domain links serve malware payloads.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-0257 Vulnerability Scanner Positive
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'CVE-2026-0257 — match against your vulnerability scanner' and recommends hunts. Pipeline generated zero detection logic despite this direct guidance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on vulnerability scanner detections flagging CVE-2026-0257 on PAN-OS instances. Cross-correlate with patch dates and exposure status to prioritize systems with delta between detection and remediation.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized VPN Authentication Success
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability 'allows attackers to...establish an unauthorized VPN connection.' This post-bypass success condition is a direct behavioral indicator but was not translated to any detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag VPN authentication successes from IPs or principals that fail baseline policy checks (unusual geolocation, time-of-day, failed auth immediately prior, service accounts). Correlate with failed authentication attempts in the preceding hours.

suggestion.title: PAN-OS Authentication Bypass Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Core vulnerability is 'authentication bypass' but pipeline surfaces no hunt for the actual bypass mechanics (auth failures, unexpected grants, malformed requests). Article indicates this is the initial compromise vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor PAN-OS authentication logs for sequences indicating bypass (failed auth events followed immediately by successful session establishment without re-authentication, or auth logs showing unusual token issuance). Look for unauthenticated access to management interfaces.

suggestion.title: Exposed PAN-OS Management Interface Detection
suggestion.rationale: T1190 'Exploit Public-Facing Application' in article implies PAN-OS instances are internet-accessible. Pipeline did not suggest detection for management-plane exposure, which is the prerequisite for exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query for PAN-OS management interfaces (ports 443, 22, 3978) responding to internet sources. Cross-reference with asset inventory for expected internet-facing instances. Flag any unplanned exposure.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Data Flow Over Compromised VPN
suggestion.rationale: Successful VPN access establishes a command-and-control or lateral-movement pathway. Article's mention of 'bypass security restrictions' implies subsequent malicious activity post-VPN-auth. Pipeline did not model downstream impact.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor VPN sessions for anomalous data volumes, protocols, or destinations. Correlate with vulnerability scanner hits for CVE-2026-0257 to identify compromised VPN sessions that may now be exfiltrating or lateral-movement staging.

suggestion.title: Botnet C2 Communication to Seized Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article states 200 servers 'controlled computers, tablets, and smartphones to carry out cyberattacks.' Organizations should detect outbound beacons to these C2 nodes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on egress connections from endpoints to known botnet C2 server IPs (200 seized Netherlands infrastructure). Monitor for periodic callbacks with small payloads, abnormal port usage, or encrypted command channels characteristic of botnet heartbeats.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized Proxy Client Software Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'owners of the devices...did not knowingly participate,' indicating malicious proxy client installation. 'Platform offers corporate, residential, and mobile proxies'—infected devices ran undisclosed client.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect installation and persistence of Asocks or similar residential proxy software. Monitor for process execution of proxy binaries, scheduled task/registry persistence mechanisms, and suspicious parent-child relationships (system processes spawning proxy clients).

suggestion.title: Default Credential Exploitation on IoT/Network Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article mitigation guidance: 'ensure the default credentials have been changed.' Infection vector implied weak device authentication across 17M devices.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor network devices (routers, modems, IoT) for login attempts with default factory credentials. Alert on successful authentication using unchanged credentials or patterns of rapid failed attempts across multiple devices (credential spraying on network segments).

suggestion.title: Residential Proxy DDoS/Abuse Traffic Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Article: botnet used for 'distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, malicious traffic proxying.' Detection of weaponized proxy infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound proxy traffic for anomalous patterns: single source IP making high-volume requests to diverse targets, rapid user-agent rotation, or request timing inconsistent with human behavior. Flag residential proxy services abused in DDoS campaigns or credential stuffing attacks.

suggestion.title: Malware Artifact & Hash Detection for Botnet Payload
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'malware botnet' infected 17M devices but provides no specific malware family. Generate detection on known botnet binaries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Build YARA/hash-based detections for botnet malware samples associated with Asocks infrastructure. Monitor for unsigned or suspicious process execution spawning network communication, memory injection, or credential theft behaviors typical of botnet payloads.

suggestion.title: Hosting Provider Infrastructure Lateral Movement
suggestion.rationale: Article: '200 servers used to host the infrastructure were located in the Netherlands' at 'a hosting provider.' Detect compromise of provider infrastructure itself.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: For customers of the compromised hosting provider: monitor for suspicious administrative access, cross-VM data transfers, or privilege escalation on hosted instances. Cross-reference seized C2 server IPs against corporate infrastructure communications.

suggestion.title: Prototype pollution property access in vm2 sandbox context
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes exploit via `Buffer.call.call({}.__lookupGetter__, Buffer, "__proto__")` and `__lookupSetter__` patterns. No hunt targets the actual code pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Node.js processes executing vm2 code that accesses `__proto__`, `__lookupGetter__`, `__lookupSetter__` via property getter/setter chains. This is the core sandbox-escape technique. Look for process argument containing vm2-related flags combined with prototype chain manipulation patterns.

suggestion.title: ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE error generation followed by TypeError constructor leakage
suggestion.rationale: Article states attacker 'combines… Node.js's `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` Error' to obtain host `TypeError` constructor. This error-based privilege escalation is the mechanism; no hunt captures this exploit pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for deliberately-triggered `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE` errors within vm2 sandbox context immediately followed by constructor-access attempts. Rare in legitimate code; should spike alerts on co-occurrence.

suggestion.title: Unexpected module injection or require() chain in vm2-spawned child process
suggestion.rationale: Post-escape, attacker will load host modules (e.g., `mainModule.require` mentioned in article PoC). Current hunts ignore the module-load phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect when node.exe loads unexpected modules (child_process, fs, os) immediately after vm2 invocation or shell spawn. Cross-reference against legitimate npm package dependency trees.

suggestion.title: vm2 package downgrade or pinning to vulnerable version in package.json
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain risk: developers may deliberately pin or downgrade to vulnerable version if unaware. No hunt for package manifest changes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for modifications to package.json, package-lock.json, yarn.lock that specify vm2 versions < 3.11.4. Flag any pinning of vm2 without active development justification.

suggestion.title: WAF/proxy rejection of vm2 exploitation payloads with secondary enum of fallback patterns
suggestion.rationale: UC_22_2 detects one PoC string set; attackers will obfuscate or use alternate syntax. Need polymorphic detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Beyond literal string matching, detect JavaScript obfuscation + prototype manipulation (e.g., base64-encoded payload + constructor.constructor + eval). Group alerts by source IP to catch reconnaissance.

suggestion.title: Nodejs process spawning unexpected child with file-system write to sensitive locations post-exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Kill-chain must include post-breach artifact creation (backdoor, config modification). Current hunts only check shell spawn, not persistence indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate node.exe child-shell spawn (UC_22_3 trigger) with file writes to /etc, /var, Windows system directories, or scheduled task creation within 60 seconds. This signals impact beyond sandbox escape.

suggestion.title: vm2 NodeVM instantiation with nesting:true and missing require option—vulnerable configuration pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'nesting:true without explicit require still allows full RCE'. The vulnerability is specific to code pattern `new NodeVM({nesting: true})` without the `require` field specified. No hunt detects this configuration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for source code patterns matching NodeVM instantiation with nesting:true but no require option. Parse npm package.json, app.js, and index.js for vm2 usage. Flag instances where nesting is enabled without explicit require: false. Combine with timestamps of code deployment to detect recent introduction of vulnerable patterns.

suggestion.title: Require/import resolution escape within vm2 context—child_process/fs module access attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article describes the patch bypass allowing access to blocked modules; exploitation requires code executing within the vm2 context to access require('child_process') or similar. No hunt detects actual exploitation code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor vm2 runtime errors/warnings or application logs for attempts to access restricted modules from within sandboxed code. Look for patterns like 'require is not defined' followed by module escaping attempts, or successful imports of child_process, fs, os from within vm2 context. Correlate with Node.js parent process event.

suggestion.title: vm2 package.json version inventory filtered to CVE-2026-47137 vulnerable range (≤3.11.3)
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability exists in vm2 ≤3.11.3. UC_20_3 detects presence but not version. Asset inventory must be scoped to vulnerable versions only to be actionable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Parse package.json version field in all node_modules/vm2 instances. Filter to versions ≤3.11.3. Prioritize internet-facing Node.js applications (web frameworks, API servers, LLM execution environments). Cross-reference with running process tree to identify which hosts have vulnerable vm2 loaded in active process memory.

suggestion.title: LLM integration or code-execution-as-a-service pattern with vm2 deployment—attack surface proxy
suggestion.rationale: Article title emphasizes 'nesting:true' which is a vm2 setting used in LLM sandboxing contexts (allowing nested VM calls). Most exploitation risk is in web-facing LLM services; attacks likely target these. Generic vm2 detection misses context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify Node.js applications that are (1) internet-facing (listening on 0.0.0.0 or public IP, port 80/443/3000/5000), (2) running with vm2 module loaded, and (3) receiving inbound HTTP POST/GET requests to code-execution or 'eval' endpoints. Combine with process spawn behavior (UC_20_2) to detect exploitation attempts against these services specifically.

suggestion.title: CVE-2023-37903 fix bypass indicators—options.require type confusion (undefined vs false)
suggestion.rationale: Article root cause: 'check uses strict equality (options.require === false)' but attacker omits require option entirely, making it undefined. Detection should look for code patterns exploiting this type confusion or code review of vulnerable instances.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan application code for vm2/NodeVM instantiation where the require option is not explicitly specified. Flag cases where nesting:true is set but require is missing (not set to false). Code review tool integration: report lines where NodeVM constructor is called with nesting but missing require parameter.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-47140 vulnerable vm2 inventory — denylist bypass surface detection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'NodeVM blocks several dangerous Node.js builtins...However, the denylist misses process and inspector/promises'. Explicit IOC 'CVE-2026-47140' under Indicators section. UC_18_2 in article shows this hunt maps to 'weapon' phase with high confidence. Pipeline generated zero IOCs or version-match detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for npm/vm2 package with SoftwareVersion matching regex ^3.(?:[0-9]|10|11.[0-3])(?:\.|$) or direct CVE-2026-47140 flag in vulnerability scans. Prioritize internet-facing systems running Node.js application stacks.

suggestion.title: NodeVM denylist bypass PoC keyword hunt — getBuiltinModule and inspector/promises access
suggestion.rationale: Article directly states attack mechanism: 'Both [process and inspector/promises] can be used from sandboxed code to reach host-side execution primitives.' UC_18_4 identifies concrete bypass patterns: 'getBuiltinModule', 'inspector/promises', 'Runtime.evaluate', 'require(\'process\').getBuiltinModule'. These are attack-specific IOC-like strings Pipeline completely missed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for process command lines or code files (.js, .mjs, .cjs) containing bypass pattern strings when executed or created by Node.js process. Alert if these patterns appear outside legitimate npm/yarn/pnpm package manager contexts.

suggestion.title: Node.js spawning native shell interpreter post-denylist escape
suggestion.rationale: Article describes impact: 'allows sandboxed code to bypass the intended builtin restrictions and execute code in the host process.' UC_18_3 targets post-exploit behavior—Node.js parent spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, wmic, etc. Pipeline generated zero impact-phase detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process creation where InitiatingProcessFileName matches 'node.exe' or 'node' and child FileName is native shell interpreter (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, bash, sh, wmic.exe, etc.) spawned by non-system account. Reduce FP by excluding npm/yarn/pnpm cache/bin directories.

suggestion.title: Sandboxed code module enumeration — process.getBuiltinModule access patterns
suggestion.rationale: Article core attack: 'The denylist misses process and inspector/promises.' T1480 (Execution Guardrails) maps to circumventing sandbox restrictions. Detection should target attempts to enumerate or access forbidden builtin modules that bypass the NodeVM denylist.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Node.js process for calls to require('process').getBuiltinModule(), require('inspector/promises'), or direct module.builtinModules enumeration when running under sandboxed/isolated context. Alert on access patterns that bypass documented NodeVM restrictions.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable NodeVM/vm2 application deployment in production
suggestion.rationale: Article vulnerability: CVE-2026-47140 affects deployed applications using vm2 ≤3.11.3 for code sandboxing. T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) applies. Detection should identify running applications with vulnerable dependencies before exploitation occurs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Asset discovery hunt: identify Node.js applications with package.json or package-lock.json dependencies on vm2 with vulnerable version range. Cross-reference with Shodan/internet-facing assets. Alert on applications accepting user-controlled script input to sandboxed vm2 context.

suggestion.title: vm2 Promise.prototype constructor manipulation – runtime behavior
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'localPromise constructor... calling this.then(undefined, eater)... missing a call to resetPromiseSpecies to ensure that this has no special species.' UC_21_3 only fingerprints PoC source strings; none monitor the actual Promise constructor chain manipulation (Symbol.species binding, .then() chaining) during sandbox execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor node.exe for Symbol.species getters/setters on Promise.prototype, custom .then() implementations that circumvent resetPromiseSpecies, or constructor property access chains that precede child_process spawning by <5 seconds.

suggestion.title: Code injection into vm2 sandbox – initial access & delivery
suggestion.rationale: Article describes vulnerable vm2 accepting attacker code ('attackers to write code which can escape from the VM2 sandbox') but no UC hunts how that code reaches the vm2 instance. Missing detection for vm2 code loading from untrusted sources, script injection via API, or file-based code drops preceding execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect node.exe or npm.exe processes loading or executing .js/.mjs files immediately before spawn of child processes, especially when sources are user-controlled (web uploads, API request bodies, temp files).

suggestion.title: WebAssembly JSPI API invocation from untrusted code context
suggestion.rationale: Article states attack vector is 'JSPI-backed Promise' via 'WebAssembly.promising' / 'WebAssembly.Suspending'. No detection for suspicious WebAssembly API calls in vm2-hosted code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Node.js processes that load WebAssembly modules containing JSPI-enabled sections followed by Promise-species manipulation. Correlate vm2 module instantiation with WebAssembly.promising() calls. This is difficult at endpoint level but critical for environments where untrusted WASM is executed in sandboxes.

suggestion.title: vm2 sandbox import followed by untrusted code execution with async/Promise context
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies vulnerability requires 'async support' and 'Promise.finally()'. Pipeline missed the behavioral requirement that vm2 + async execution is the precondition.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate vm2 package import/require event + Node process with command-line flags enabling async contexts (e.g., --experimental-async or custom runner scripts). Behavioral correlation reduces false positives vs. bare vm2 presence.

suggestion.title: vm2 version inventory and exposure quantification
suggestion.rationale: Article states affected versions: ≤3.11.3. Pipeline should have flagged all instances for remediation planning, not just detection. Missing software-inventory use case.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Inventory all Node.js projects with vm2 in package.json or node_modules. Parse version from package-lock.json or installed artifacts. Flag instances with version ≤3.11.3 for immediate remediation or isolation.

suggestion.title: Promise.prototype.finally() species bypass indicators in JavaScript bytecode/source
suggestion.rationale: Article core attack: 'bypasses expected Promise-species hardening' via '.finally()'. No detection for malicious Promise hardening bypass patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: In code-review or SAST context: flag Promise.finally() calls in untrusted code that attempt to override Promise.prototype or manipulate constructor/species. In forensic analysis: inspect heap for Promise objects with modified species property or corrupted internal slots.

suggestion.title: Node.js process environment modification indicative of sandbox escape
suggestion.rationale: Post-exploitation (T1068 → T1611), the attacker has host environment access. Article describes 'arbitrary code execution in the host process'. Detection should flag Node process that modifies global/environment state or spawns children with elevated privilege.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Node.exe spawning children with different privilege level (e.g., SYSTEM, NETWORK SERVICE) or modifying HKLM registry. Correlate with vm2 being active in parent. Flag as sandbox-escape indicator.

suggestion.title: PraisonAI subprocess with print.__self__ introspection + credential/privilege discovery commands
suggestion.rationale: Article states attacker uses 'print.__self__' to retrieve builtins, then achieves OS command execution. Post-exploitation involves discovery commands (id, whoami) and credential reads (/etc/passwd, env vars). Current UC_8_6 detects signature in isolation; UC_8_5 detects discovery in isolation. Combining both (literal exploit trigger + behavioral follow-up) reduces FP and increases confidence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on sequences: Python process execution of 'print.__self__' or '__self__.vars' within 30 seconds of same process spawning shell (sh/bash/cmd) that immediately executes privilege discovery (id, whoami, sudo) or credential enumeration (printenv, cat /etc/passwd, env). Require both components to fire.

suggestion.title: Discovery commands bulk-executed by Python subprocess (post-exploitation enumeration)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attacker running multiple discovery commands after sandbox escape: 'id', 'whoami', 'uname -a', 'hostname', 'cat /etc/passwd', '/proc/self/environ'. Current UC_8_5 lists these as keyword matches but lacks sequence/frequency context. Legitimate Python scripts rarely execute 3+ distinct discovery commands in <60 seconds.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate Python parent process spawning 3+ distinct shell child processes executing discovery commands (id, whoami, uname, hostname, cat /etc/passwd) within 60-second window. Flag if process parent is not in whitelist (legitimate data-science tools, CI/CD orchestrators).

suggestion.title: Environment variable + credential file exfiltration from Python subprocess
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly lists post-exploitation activities: 'printenv', 'cat /etc/passwd', 'AWS_SECRET', 'AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET', 'OPENAI_API_KEY', '/run/secrets', '/var/run/secrets'. Should detect credential enumeration followed by network exfiltration (curl/wget to external IP, DNS tunnel, or in-memory credential staging).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert if Python spawns child shell that reads credential sources (/etc/shadow, ~/.ssh, AWS credential files, Kubernetes secrets at /run/secrets) followed by network connection to external IP or curl/wget child process with credential-like strings in CLI.

suggestion.title: Application code path: untrusted input routed to PraisonAI execute_code()
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies vulnerability in execute_code() function. Exploitation requires the vulnerable code to be reachable with untrusted input. Should detect application-layer ingestion: user input submitted to LLM framework that invokes execute_code() with user-controlled payload.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor application logs for: execute_code() invocation with user-supplied data; code strings containing exploit pattern 'print.__self__'; unusual code submission sizes or obfuscated payloads; or HTTP POST/PUT requests to PraisonAI agent endpoints with Python code containing introspection builtins.

suggestion.title: PraisonAI generated server lacks authentication middleware validation
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'authentication disabled by default'—this is the core vulnerability, but no UC explicitly hunts for the *absence* of auth checks in Flask config, generated `api.py`, or running process environment. The phrase 'authentication disabled' suggests looking for missing JWT tokens, disabled Flask-Login, or unchecked request handlers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for creation or modification of Flask `api.py` or app config files that omit authentication decorators (e.g., `@app.before_request` checks, `requires_auth()`). Cross-reference process memory (if available) or file content for `authentication_enabled: false` or absence of credential validation in `/chat` and `/agents` route handlers.

suggestion.title: Public source probing PraisonAI `/agents` endpoint for LLM agent enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions exposed `/agents` endpoint but UC_9_5 conflates `/chat` and `/agents` as a single behavioral pattern. Agents endpoint is distinct—likely returns a list of deployed agents. Reconnaissance-phase probing (GET requests, no body) differs from exploitation (POST with payloads).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect GET requests to `/agents` from public sources; anomalous user-agents (scanners, bot names); requests in bursts (enumeration sweeps); or responses with 200-OK status revealing agent names/metadata.

suggestion.title: PraisonAI deployment YAML configuration exposing bind address 0.0.0.0
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'binds to 0.0.0.0 per the recommended sample YAML'—the vulnerable config itself is the IOC. No UC hunts for the presence of misconfigurations in YAML files or environment variables that override Flask's default bind address.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for PraisonAI YAML config files (e.g., `praison_config.yaml`, `deploy.yaml`) containing `host: 0.0.0.0` or `bind: 0.0.0.0`, or process command lines with Flask env vars setting `FLASK_ENV=0.0.0.0`. Compare to expected internal bind addresses (127.0.0.1, or known LAN IPs).

suggestion.title: Workspace owner role removal — targeted demotion immediately before escalation
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'promote themselves or others to owner'—implies potential demotion of legitimate owners. The attack chain would be: (1) identify current owner(s), (2) demote them, (3) promote attacker. UC_4_3 detects the chain but not the targeting phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Within workspace, detect role-change PATCH requests that target the same user_id multiple times OR that target all users with 'owner' role in rapid succession. Baseline: how often does a legitimate member change owner roles vs. a non-owner?

suggestion.title: Workspace-wide member enumeration before or after privilege escalation
suggestion.rationale: Article omits enumeration tactics. To escalate, attacker must first list members to identify targets. GET /workspaces/{id}/members or similar enumeration endpoint before first PATCH would be pre-exploit reconnaissance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect GET requests to /workspaces/*/members* endpoints followed within 5 minutes by PATCH /workspaces/*/members/* with role change. Successful 200s/204s in both sequences.

suggestion.title: Account access removal — legitimate-owner lockout post-escalation
suggestion.rationale: T1531 (Account Access Removal) is listed but no hunt captures it. If attacker demotes or disables legitimate owners after self-promotion, that's an account-lockout signal: PATCH with role='none' or DELETE /workspaces/{id}/members/{legitimate_owner_id}.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect PATCH /workspaces/*/members/* requests that change a user with 'owner' or 'admin' role to 'member', 'viewer', or removal. Combine with UC_4_3 to identify demotion of the user who originally called the API.

suggestion.title: Shadow AI Tool Usage Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Providing sanctioned tools also helps reduce shadow AI by discouraging developers from turning to unmanaged consumer services.' Implies orgs without sanctioned AI tools face higher risk of unmanaged tool adoption. Detection would identify developers using non-approved AI coding assistants.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor network egress to known consumer AI service endpoints (ChatGPT, Claude free tier, etc.) from developer machines. Track API requests to unmanaged AI platforms. Alert on source code being sent to non-sanctioned services via clipboard or copy-paste patterns.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable Dependency Introduction at Scale
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'AI also accelerated the generation of insecure code and vulnerable dependencies.' Pipeline should detect patterns where AI-assisted development introduces higher velocity of vulnerable packages compared to pre-AI baseline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Compare velocity of new vulnerable dependency introductions week-over-week. Flag significant increases in vulnerable package commits. Correlate timing of AI tool adoption with vulnerability introduction rate changes.

suggestion.title: Absence of Pre-Commit Security Scanning
suggestion.rationale: Article highlights 'custom pre-commit hooks' scanning code before commit as critical gap-closer. Absence of pre-commit hooks or their bypass attempts indicates organization lacks secure-at-inception controls.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for bypassed or disabled pre-commit hooks (e.g., git commit --no-verify). Track commits pushed without pre-commit scan records. Alert when repositories lose pre-commit hook integrity.

suggestion.title: Security Findings Queue Backlog Spike
suggestion.rationale: Article notes 'Esaie was receiving five to ten developer questions every day related to security findings.' High volume of security remediation requests indicates reactive, not proactive, security posture.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor issue tracker for spike in security-tagged items assigned to security engineers. Track help queue volume for security-related questions. Alert when question rate exceeds threshold, indicating developers discovering issues too late in workflow.

suggestion.title: HTTPSpy C2 Callback Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title: 'Kimsuky Deploys HTTPSpy'—no UC generated. HTTPSpy is the primary tool deployed; absence of C2 detection is a critical gap.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HTTPSpy process execution and HTTP(S) callbacks to known Kimsuky C2 nodes. Look for persistent HTTPS connections with anomalous TLS certificate chains or beaconing intervals matching documented HTTPSpy signatures.

suggestion.title: HelloDoor Lateral Movement and Remote Shell
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions HelloDoor expansion in arsenal. No UC addresses post-compromise shell access or lateral movement artifacts HelloDoor introduces.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HelloDoor process creation, DLL injection into Windows services, and execution of cmd.exe or powershell.exe from unexpected parents. Flag lateral movement patterns consistent with HelloDoor tunneling.

suggestion.title: VS Code Tunnel Remote Access Abuse
suggestion.rationale: Article headline: 'VS Code Tunnels'—legitimate-tool weaponization for C2 or interactive access. No UC for detecting tunnel activation, relay registration, or tunnel-based code execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for code-server.exe or code (VS Code) establishing tunnel to official Microsoft relay infrastructure; flag unauthenticated users or non-standard tunnel parameters. Alert if tunnels are created outside normal dev workflows (off-hours, from system accounts, to external IPs).

suggestion.title: Kimsuky Spear-Phishing with Malware Attachment
suggestion.rationale: Kimsuky's known TTPs involve spear-phishing. Article implies new tool deployment but no UC for initial-access detection via phishing or weaponized documents.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect suspicious email attachments with YARA/hash rules for HTTPSpy and HelloDoor droppers. Flag macro-enabled docs or archives executing scripts to temp directories, especially from external senders with Kimsuky targeting indicators.

suggestion.title: Suspicious NuGet Package Installation from Untrusted Source or Unusual Package Name
suggestion.rationale: Article title: 'Malicious NuGet Package as Sicoob SDK' — supply-chain entry point. Pipeline missed initial-access detection. Attackers registered counterfeit or similarly-named package; detection must cover installation events with name mismatches or source anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor nuget.exe and dotnet.exe process execution with 'install' or 'restore' arguments. Flag packages with names closely resembling legitimate Sicoob libraries (Levenshtein distance, homoglyph variants). Alert if installed from non-standard NuGet feeds or package sources added outside change management.

suggestion.title: Credential Extraction from Windows Credential Manager by .NET Process
suggestion.rationale: Article title states 'Exfiltrates Banking Passwords' — malicious SDK must access stored credentials. Attack phrase establishes credential_access phase; pipeline reconstruction was empty.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on .NET/PowerShell processes accessing HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Vault or CredentialManager registry hives. Monitor for dpapi.dll, vaultcli.dll, or CredentialManager API calls (DPAPI decrypt operations) initiated by untrusted assemblies loaded from NuGet cache.

suggestion.title: Unsigned .NET Assembly Execution from NuGet Package Cache Directory
suggestion.rationale: Malicious SDK executes as .NET assembly from cache. Pipeline did not reconstruct execution phase. Detection gap: unsigned or untrusted assembly load from %USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages or intermediate build output.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor .NET AssemblyLoad ETW events for assemblies originating from NuGet package paths. Flag if signer thumbprint is not in trusted certificate list or assembly is unsigned. Correlate with recent nuget install or package restore events within same process.

suggestion.title: Banking Credential Exfiltration Over HTTP/HTTPS to Attacker Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article title: 'Exfiltrates Banking Passwords' — explicit exfiltration phase. Pipeline failed to map this to T1041 or generate network-based detection. Malicious SDK beacons credential data to attacker C2.
